title: Agentic AI Startup RevRag.AI Nets $2.5 Mn To Build AI Relationship Managers For Lenders And Insurers
content: Agentic AI startup RevRag.AI has raised $2.5 Mn (about ₹24 Cr) in a seed funding round led by Accion Ventures to expedite product development and expand to the US market. Cedar Hill Capital, Wyser and Venture Catalysts have also backed the startup. “From the perspective of financial services, the US has a vast number of companies from insurance to credit cards to loans. There is huge penetration there and a large market. And we see that there’s not much competition yet in the category we’re building in,” cofounder and CEO Ashutosh Singh told Inc42 in an interaction. While expanding to the US market appears to be on the top of the list, the startup is also looking to invest further in fine-tuning its own multimodal small language models (SLMs) to bring its tech layers in-house. Important to highlight that all of its platform is built on third-party proprietary models. Singh, with schoolmates Neeraj Gupta and Pankaj Gupta, had founded Revrag in 2023 initially modelled as a savings-oriented fintech platform. The idea of pivoting to a SaaS platform came when the trio realised that, while fintech users have slick interfaces and fast transactions at their disposal, onboarding customers continues to be bogged down by repetitive data entry, multiple verifications and cumbersome documentation. Pivoting early in 2025, RevRag.AI now aims to bridge this gap by streamlining onboarding and sales for banks and fintechs. For this, it offers autonomous AI agents that are capable enough to act as virtual relationship managers embedded within the financial institutions app. Beyond onboarding, the AI agents also automate customer product sales, support functions as well as provide real-time, multilingual assistance. This helps minimise conversion drop-offs, particularly when it comes to users from underserved backgrounds who have limited trust in digital systems and need assistance navigating financial terminology or English interfaces. As per Singh, RevRag’s offerings can save up to 70% of costs when compared to traditional channels while simultaneously helping in revenue generation. Thus, the startup will remain sharply focused on this problem statement rather than expanding into additional use cases. Earlier in 2025 , the startup had told Inc42 that it was mulling to launch a no-code flow builder and expand its presence in Indian and American BFSI markets. The startup has shared aspirations to touch an annual recurring revenue of $50 Mn by FY28. It has lined up innovations like AI-led cross-selling, real-time risk scoring, and automated claims handling. As of now, it serves over 45 customers across India including the likes of PhonePe, Razorpay, Bajaj Finance, Motilal Oswal, and IIFL. It earlier raised $1 Mn from Powerhouse Ventures and various angel investors including WhatsApp head Kunal Shah. The fresh round comes at a time when the use of AI in automating fintech business functions is picking up. The global AI in fintech market is pegged to be valued at $45.53 Bn in 2026 and is projected to cross $241 Bn by 2034, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 23.20%. title: UC Hungry For Funds Again, DailyObjects’ D2C Playbook & More
content: UC Taps Public Markets Again for Funds Urban Company is hungry for more cash. Despite sitting on over hundreds of crores in cash, the consumer services giant’s board will convene next week to consider a fresh fundraise. So, why is Urban Company heading back to the public markets less than a year after its IPO? UC Seeks Fresh Capital: The startup’s board will meet on October 16 to consider raising capital through equity shares or convertible securities. Besides this, the board will also take a call on which route to take for the fundraise. But what makes this episode interesting is that UC was sitting on ₹2,019 Cr in cash and treasury investments at the end of June. Even ₹310.8 Cr of the startup’s ₹472 Cr fresh issue also remains unutilised. So, why is it chasing more money? The Cash Guzzler: The likely pressure point is InstaHelp, UC’s instant services vertical. The company is investing heavily in the new arm to create a new category as competition continues to intensify from Snabbit and Pronto. On top of this, InstaHelp continues to weigh heavily on UC’s overall profitability, reporting an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹132 Cr in Q1 FY27. Management expects InstaHelp to remain loss-making for the next few years and is unlikely to achieve breakeven before FY31 A Wider Trend: Urban Company’s post-IPO fundraise move reflects a broader pattern among listed new-age tech companies . For companies still investing in expansion, secondary issuances offer capital without interest obligations or repayment pressure. Strong share prices can also allow businesses to raise more money with less dilution. Rather than viewing an IPO as a final exit, founders are using public markets as an ongoing liquidity engine. But, investors are also shifting focus from gross revenue to earnings per share and ROIC to ensure fresh money creates genuine accretion rather than capital hoarding. Amid this backdrop, will Urban Company’s latest fundraise find any takers? Let’s find out… From The Editor’s Desk DailyObjects’ Slow-Burn Playbook From selling smartphone cases in 2014 to selling accessories and bags, DailyObjects has come a long way in the past decade. What has helped the brand move beyond a market dominated by low-cost, unbranded accessories is its design-led differentiation. The startup reported a revenue of ₹200 Cr in FY26, and is targeting a ₹400 Cr top line and EBITDA profitability in FY27. This has come on the back of a richer product mix, greater offline contribution and supply-chain efficiencies. DailyObjects also currently operates 13 exclusive brand outlets and is present in 300 Apple premium reseller stores. It plans to open two to three stores a month, add 30–35 stores in FY27 and build a network of 150–160 stores over five years. GreenCell Bags ₹330 Cr The EV startup has raised $34.6 Mn in an equity funding round led by Impact Fund Denmark to support the rollout of about 4,500 electric buses, execute its order book and streamline service delivery. Founded in 2019, GreenCell Mobility acquires e-buses from contract manufacturers and then deploys them for both intercity and intracity travel. It claims to operate more than 1,200 electric buses and runs over 270 charging stations. It has raised $37 Mn to date. The fundraise comes as the homegrown electric bus ecosystem continues to scale rapidly on the back of growing government procurement, GCC models, rising EV adoption and electric transition mandates. UPI MDR Saga Continues The National Payments Corporation of India has deferred the re-introduction of merchant discount rate on select UPI transactions. Instead of the earlier October 15 rollout, the MDR will now be implemented “immediately after Diwali”. The NPCI said it took the decision keeping the festive season in mind. The revised implementation date will be notified separately. This follows reports that the Centre was considering delaying the MDR rollout to January 2027. Under the proposed framework, merchants would be charged an MDR of 0.40% on P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 per transaction. The move had invited significant push back from retailers, which had demanded the rollback of MDR. DealShare CEO Exits Kamaldeep Singh has stepped down as the CEO of the troubled ecommerce unicorn after a three year-long stint. He has now joined electric mobility solutions provider Indofast Energy as its new CEO. DealShare has not announced Singh’s replacement. The exit comes amid a slew of departures at the beleaguered ecommerce unicorn. CFO Ashish Shah is also looking to exit the startup, while DealShare’s founding team – Sourjyendu Medda, Vineet Rao, Sankar Bora and Rajat Shikhar – all exited in 2024. Known for online grocery delivery in tier-II+ cities, DealShare is trying to douse fires on multiple fronts. The startup has been scaling down its operations as online business has dwindled to “next to zero”. It is also in talks with Truemeds for a potential fire sale. Freshworks To Acquire Torii The Nasdaq-listed SaaS major has signed a definitive agreement to acquire the SaaS management platform for an undisclosed amount. Freshworks expects the deal to close by 2026-end. By integrating Torii’s SaaS management capabilities into Freshservice, the listed giant aims to help its clients have a better visibility of their AI usage and spending. Founded in 2010, Freshworks offers SaaS tools to help enterprises manage customer engagement, sales, IT service management, marketing and automation. It reported a net profit of $3.2 Mn in the quarter ended June 2026 against a revenue of $237.4 Mn. Inc42 Markets Inc42 Startup Spotlight How Lickicious Is Betting Big On India’s Pet Parents India’s pet parents want more than generic kibble or home-cooked meals. Yet, specialised and nutrition-led options remain limited. To solve this, Lickicious is building a pet nutrition brand around food, treats and supplements for dogs and cats. A Desi Pet Brand: Founded in 2024, Lickicious sells dry and wet foods, treats, supplements and nutritional toppers for dogs and cats. It positions its products around palatability and balanced nutrition, while the startup also operates its own manufacturing setup. Owning The Supply Chain: Unlike brands that rely entirely on contract manufacturing, Lickicious runs its own manufacturing setup and is developing a 60,000 sq ft manufacturing and distribution footprint. The startup claims that this will increase production capacity, improve supply reliability and strengthen quality control. The Road Ahead: Backed by Prath Ventures, the startup now plans to scale its R&D and expand into new categories, formats, species and sales channels. The brand is targeting ₹100 Cr in annual revenue going forward and aims to become one of the biggest pet food companies in the country over the next decade. With India’s pet food market projected to become a $2.2 Bn opportunity by 2030, can Lickicious scale into a durable pet food brand for dogs and cats? title: Mesa School Bags ₹110 Cr To Launch New On-Campus Courses
content: Bengaluru-based Mesa School of Business has raised ₹110 Cr ($11.4 Mn) in its Series A funding round in a mix of debt and equity. The round pegged the business school at a post-money valuation of ₹385 Cr ($40 Mn), cofounder Ankit Agarwal told Inc42. While the ₹85 Cr equity round was co-led by Dharana Capital and existing backer Elevation Capital, the remaining ₹25 Cr was raised via venture debt from InnoVen Capital and Alteria Capital. Mesa plans to utilise the fresh capital to strengthen its leadership team, integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into its programmes, deepen partnerships with startups and launch new courses. Founded in 2023 by Agarwal and Varun Limaye, Mesa offers on-campus educational programmes for individuals. It currently offers three full-time programmes targeting early-career professionals, fresh graduates and undergraduate students. While the startup charges ₹25.4 Lakh in tuition fees for its one-year post-graduate programme, its one-year Forge programme for fresh graduates has a starting fees of ₹15.4 Lakh. The undergraduate programme costs ₹48 Lakh over four years. Training Talent For Startups Despite being one of India’s fastest-growing employment segments, the local startup ecosystem continues to face a talent gap. Speaking with Inc42, Agarwal said that the talent paucity is especially acute in non-technical roles, which account for nearly 80% of jobs in the sector. While graduates from premier institutions often have established recruitment pathways into startups, students without access to such networks, Agarwal said, lack a structured route to enter the startup ecosystem. “If you want to go and work in a startup, there is no one place which sort of builds the right network,” he said. Unlike conventional business schools, Mesa does not employ full-time faculty, relying instead on startup founders, executives and industry experts to design and deliver its curriculum. Around 2,000 industry professionals have interacted with our students in some capacity, Agarwal said. “The institutions just don’t have the capability or the incentives to keep changing their curriculum and to keep it super agile over time, and that’s where we felt that we should come in and create talent for the startup ecosystem across levels and functions,” Agarwal said. On the business front, Mesa’s revenue comes primarily from programme fees, which it collects annually and largely in advance. The experienced-professional postgraduate programme contributes around 40% of revenue, while the undergraduate programme accounts for 35-40%. The fresh-graduate programme contributes around 20%, according to Agarwal. While the startup is yet to achieve profitability, founder Agarwal claims that most of Mesa’s programmes are approaching operational breakeven. Mesa claims to have grown its business around 2.5X annually over the past two years, Agarwal said, projecting that it will continue to grow at a similar pace in upcoming years. Where Are Mesa Graduates Headed? Mesa claims that its first three postgraduate cohorts have produced around 300 alumni, who have joined more than 120 startups. The startup claims that its graduates take up roles across founders’ offices, product management, partnerships, account management and venture capital. Agarwal claims that the experienced-professional postgraduate programme reports average salaries of ₹26-28 LPA. He also claimed that Mesa has so far incubated more than 50 student startups, which have clocked ₹50 Cr in annual revenue. The school also claims to provide equity-free grants and incubation support to student ventures. This comes three years after Mesa last raised ₹34 Cr in a round led by Elevation Capital in 2023 to launch its startup leadership programme. Angel investors such as CRED’s Kunal Shah, Meesho’s Vidit Aatrey, and Urban Company’s Abhiraj Bahl also participated in the round. Mesa operates in an emerging segment of alternative business education, competing most directly with Gurugram-based Masters’ Union, which combines industry-led management programmes with entrepreneurship support. Masters’ Union recently received full university status from the Haryana government. Other competitors in re-skilling and upskilling space include upGrad, Great Learning, Masai School, Eruditus and Springboard, among others. title: [Update] Blume, Speciale Invest & 11 Other AIFs Selected For Deploying ₹7,131 Cr Under RDI Fund
content: Original | Oct 14, 02:37 IST The government has selected Blume Ventures, Speciale Invest, Chiratae Ventures and 16 others as second-level fund managers (SLFM) for deploying ₹7,131 Cr from the ₹1 Lakh Cr research, development and innovation (RDI) fund. This is the first cohort of the SLFM under the fund. Overall, the empowered group of secretaries (EGoS) under the science ministry has approved 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs) for this purpose earlier this month. The other selected AIFs also include YourNest Capital Advisors, Sixth Sense Ventures, Celesta India, AdvantEdge Investment Managers, IvyCap Ventures, Ideaspring Capital Fund, TVS Capital Funds, AMA Capital Advisors, Translation Endeavors and “Campus”. Meanwhile, the selected FROs include the likes of IISc Bengaluru’s AI & Robotics Technology Park (ARTPARK), Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (CCAMP) in Bengaluru, IIT-Madras Research Park, Pilani Innovation & Entrepreneurship Development Society (PIEDS) at BITS-Pilani, and Society for Innovation & Entrepreneurship (SINE) at IIT-Bombay. Update | Oct 12, 21:48 IST Central government-backed ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund has approved 19 second-level fund managers (SLFMs) with a total commitment of ₹7,131 Cr. The Ministry of Science and Technology’s Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS) approved 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs) for this purpose earlier this month, the ministry announced. The selected entities will channel capital from the RDI Fund to eligible technology enterprises undertaking research, development and innovation activities at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 and above. The fund managers are also expected to mobilise private capital equivalent to the RDI Fund’s contribution, potentially expanding the pool of financing available to research-driven businesses. Alongside approving the first cohort of fund managers, the EGoS approved five additional technologies for coverage under the RDI Fund. The government did not specify these technologies in its announcement. The government said it would continue inviting applications and onboarding additional cohorts of fund managers, expanding the reach of the scheme and encouraging public-private investment in India’s research and innovation ecosystem. Launched in November 2025, the RDI Scheme has an overall outlay of ₹1 Lakh Cr and aims to address the funding gap faced by companies developing high-risk, high-impact technologies. It is managed by an independent business unit housed within the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST). The fund is designed to spur private investment in research-intensive businesses. However, its impact on investor sentiment, however, remains unclear. In August, The Indian Express reported that nearly two-thirds of the more than ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies under the scheme had gone to firms linked to members of the panel involved in selecting beneficiaries. The report raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest. Inc42’s Q3 2026 Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, which covered 85 institutional investors, found that 52% considered disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate, but said visibility into the process remained limited. Another 25% viewed the issue as a governance failure that required independent oversight, while 14% said potential conflicts could be managed through disclosure and recusal. The remaining 9% said the issue was not a concern, arguing that the focus should be on selecting the right companies. As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startup funding in the September quarter zoomed 176% YoY to $290 Mn raised across 28 deals , compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. The sector outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn. title: Founder Salaries Tracker FY26: How Much Did India’s Startup Founders Earn?
content: Nineteen founders across 13 new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹52.57 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 2% from ₹51.54 Cr in FY25, according to data compiled by Inc42. Average fixed remuneration per founder increased to ₹2.76 Cr from ₹2.71 Cr. Of these, 13 founders received increases in fixed pay, four saw reductions, and two reported unchanged remuneration. Honasa Consumer cofounder Ghazal Alagh recorded the highest percentage increase, with her fixed remuneration rising 60% to ₹2.4 Cr from ₹1.5 Cr. Delhivery cofounder Sahil Barua followed with a 21.4% increase to ₹3.4 Cr from ₹2.8 Cr. Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal recorded the steepest percentage decline, with his remuneration falling 34.8% to ₹4.5 Cr from ₹6.9 Cr. Nykaa founder Falguni Nayar’s fixed pay fell 14% to ₹74 Lakh from ₹86 Lakh, while Swiggy cofounder Sriharsha Majety’s remuneration declined 12.5% to ₹1.4 Cr from ₹1.6 Cr. Lenskart cofounder Peyush Bansal drew the highest fixed remuneration among the founders tracked, despite a 1.7% decline to ₹5.7 Cr from ₹5.8 Cr. Meesho cofounders Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar followed with ₹4.8 Cr each, ahead of Ola Electric’s Aggarwal at ₹4.5 Cr and Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma at ₹4 Cr. Sharma’s fixed remuneration remained unchanged from FY25. However, fixed pay tells only part of the story. Peyush Bansal received ₹12 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives – more than twice his fixed remuneration – along with perquisites and retirement benefits. Fellow Lenskart cofounder Neha Bansal received ₹6 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives, in addition to her ₹2.7 Cr fixed pay. Share-based compensation also featured prominently. Majety’s ESOP gains stood at ₹549.3 Cr, while Delhivery cofounder Kapil Bharati recorded ₹6.9 Cr in ESOP gains. Separately, the cost of stock options granted to FirstCry founder Supam Maheshwari stood at ₹31.7 Cr. He also received ₹2.1 Cr in perquisites and ₹84 Lakh in performance incentives. These components require separate treatment. Stock-option costs and ESOP-related benefits do not necessarily represent cash received by a founder during the year and should be distinguished from fixed salaries and cash incentives. Inc42 has been tracking founders’ remuneration since FY23, covering the startup ecosystem’s shift from the era of funding boom to the funding winter and now, more recently, towards profitability and IPOs. Building on the FY25 edition , the FY26 tracker examines changes in fixed pay, other compensation components, and the financial performance of the companies these founders lead. In addition to his fixed pay, Bansal also received ₹12 Cr in bonus and performance incentives, along with ₹24.04 Lakh in perquisites and ₹7.5 Lakh in retirals. Lenskart’s net profit rose 69% YoY to ₹500.9 Cr in FY26, while operating revenue increased 33% YoY to ₹8,814 Cr. Its profit growth was aided by operating leverage, premiumisation, and growth in international markets. Vidit Aatrey & Sanjeev Kumar | Meesho Meesho cofounders Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar each earned ₹4.8 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 6.7% from ₹4.5 Cr a year earlier. The data reviewed by Inc42 did not disclose additional perks for either founder. The ecommerce company’s operating revenue increased 34.5% YoY to ₹12,626 Cr in FY26, while its net loss narrowed 65.6% YoY to ₹1,357.7 Cr. Its annual transacting user base grew 33% YoY to 26.4 Cr in Q4 FY26, while order volumes increased 43% YoY to 71.7 Cr during the quarter. Bhavish Aggarwal | Ola Electric Ola Electric founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal earned ₹4.5 Cr in remuneration in FY26, compared with ₹6.9 Cr in FY25. In FY26, the EV maker’s net loss narrowed nearly 20% to ₹1,833 Cr from ₹2,276 Cr in the previous fiscal. Operating revenue nearly halved to ₹2,460 Cr from ₹4,932 Cr. Sahil Barua & Kapil Bharati | Delhivery Delhivery cofounders Sahil Barua and Kapil Bharati earned ₹3.4 Cr and ₹3.3 Cr, respectively, in fixed remuneration in FY26. Barua’s fixed pay increased 21.4% from ₹2.8 Cr in FY25, while Bharati’s rose 17.9% from ₹2.8 Cr. In addition, Barua received ₹33.7 Lakh in performance incentives. Bharati received ₹33 Lakh in performance incentives and ₹6.9 Cr in ESOP gains. The logistics company’s operating revenue rose 17% YoY to ₹10,486 Cr in FY26, while net profit grew 8% YoY to ₹321 Cr. Vijay Shekhar Sharma | Paytm Paytm founder and CEO Vijay Shekhar Sharma earned ₹4 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, unchanged from the previous year. He also received ₹33 Lakh in perquisites. The fintech company reported its first full-year net profit of ₹552 Cr in FY26, compared with a loss of ₹663 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue increased 22.3% YoY to ₹8,437 Cr. It also posted an EBITDA of ₹502 Cr, against an EBITDA loss of ₹1,506 Cr in the previous year. Tarun Mehta & Swapnil Jain | Ather Ather Energy cofounders Tarun Mehta and Swapnil Jain each earned ₹2.1 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 5% from ₹2 Cr a year earlier. They also received ₹90 Lakh each in variable compensation, taking their individual fixed and variable pay to ₹3 Cr. The EV maker’s operating revenue rose 62.8% YoY to ₹3,671.8 Cr, while its net loss narrowed 36.3% YoY to ₹517.2 Cr. EBITDA loss declined 51.6% YoY to ₹257 Cr, with its EBITDA margin improving to -6.7% from -23% in FY25. title: Freshworks To Acquire Torii To Expand AI Spend Governance Offerings
content: Nasdaq-listed SaaS major Freshworks has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Torii, a SaaS management platform, to extend its IT service management tool, Freshservice, into AI and software spend governance. The transaction is expected to close in the quarter ending December 2026. Founded in 2017 by Uri Haramati, Uri Nativ and Tal Bereznitskey in New York, Torii helps enterprises track AI consumption at the token level, attribute usage to specific internal teams, forecast spend trajectories, and set operational budget limits. By integrating its SaaS management capabilities into Freshservice, Freshworks aims to enable organisations to have better visibility of their AI usage. The system provides IT and finance departments with continuous oversight, replacing manual spreadsheet reconciliation with real-time analytics. “Modern IT teams are being asked to govern more of the business than ever, with less visibility into what it costs. Freshservice already gives IT one place to see everything they run. With Torii, that same view now extends to software and AI spend — what’s running, who’s using it, and what it costs, so finance and IT stop reconciling spreadsheets and start making decisions together,” said Freshworks CEO and President Dennis Woodside. Founded in 2010 by Girish Mathrubootham and Shanmugam Krishnasamy, Freshworks offers a suite of cloud-based software to help companies manage customer engagement, sales, IT service management and marketing. After Mathrubootham exited the company in 2024, it has sought to reinvent itself as an AI-native enterprise platform under Woodside’s leadership. Apart from introducing AI-led offerings like vertical AI agents and workflow automation tools, it also underwent a major restructuring earlier this year, trimming 11% of its workforce or around 500 employees, citing automation of work. Growing adoption of its AI products helped Freshworks get back into the black in the quarter ended June 2026 . The company reported a net profit of $3.2 Mn as against a net loss of $1.7 Mn in the year-ago period and a net loss of $4.8 Mn in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, its revenue grew 16% YoY to $237.4 Mn. The post Freshworks To Acquire Torii To Expand AI Spend Governance Offerings appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: [Update] Adani Enterprises, Jabil Sign MoU To Set Up AI-Focused Joint Venture
content: Update | October 13, 20:00 IST Adani Group’s flagship business Adani Enterprises and US-based manufacturing company Jabil Inc have signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MoU) to establish a 50:50 joint venture for manufacturing and assembling AI and data centre equipment in India. The proposed partnership aims to produce AI racks, servers, storage, networking equipment, and power and cooling systems to cater to India’s rapidly growing data centre capacity. It targets the expanding domestic market as well as international exports. “At Adani, our vision is to expand up the AI value chain evolving from powering and hosting AI infrastructure to engineering and manufacturing the critical systems that will define the next generation of computing. Our proposed joint venture with Jabil marks a strategic step towards this future, combining Jabil’s world-class engineering and manufacturing capabilities with Adani’s integrated strengths in energy, infrastructure and data centres to help build the physical backbone of the global AI economy,” said Adani Group chairman Gautam Adani. With this MoU, the earlier agreement between Adani and Jabil has now taken a more concrete form, although its realisation remains subject to regulatory approvals and the execution of definitive agreements. Original | June 15, 22:12 IST Indian conglomerate Adani Group has partnered with US-based manufacturing company Jabil Inc to build vertically-integrated AI and data centre infrastructure in India. The two companies intend to set up multi-gigawatt manufacturing capacity in India for high-density AI racks. They will produce AI-ready hardware such as liquid-cooled AI racks, servers, storage units, and networking systems to serve the needs of global hyperscalers and enterprise data centers. Beyond computing hardware, the platform plans to manufacture supporting infrastructure components, including power distribution units, coolant distribution units, transformers, switchgears, and advanced thermal management systems. The companies are currently finalising operational frameworks and formal documentation to execute the manufacturing roadmap, with no definitive timeline announced. The partnership with Jabil is in line with Adani Group’s bid to double down on AI. In February, Adani announced one of the world’s largest integrated energy-compute commitments with a direct investment of $100 Bn to develop renewable-energy-powered, hyperscale AI-ready data centres by 2035. Later, the Adani Group was said to be exploring partnerships with Meta, Google among others, to set up data centres in the country. To note, the conglomerate has also tied up with Uber to set up its first data centre in India, which would become operational later this year. The Adani-Jabil partnership comes at a time when the global market opportunity for AI compute infrastructure is projected to zoom past the $3 Tn mark over the next seven years. India’s data centre capacity is projected to reach 5-8 GW by 2030, driven by growing AI demand, cloud expansion, and data localisation requirements. Notably, India’s technology supply chains are increasingly shifting toward domestic manufacturing, given the focus on data sovereignty and the requirements of the DPDP Act. Along with the Adani Group, companies like Reliance Industries and Amazon are also betting on capturing this momentum. For instance, Reliance announced a partnership with Meta last week that would see the oil-to-telecom conglomerate set up a 168 MW AI-enabled data centre in Gujarat’s Jamnagar , powered by sustainable energy, within two years. Amazon has committed an investment of $12.7 Bn towards cloud infrastructure in India by 2030, while OpenAI is planning to set up a 1 GW data centre in India in partnership with TCS. title: GreenCell Mobility Raises ₹330 Cr To Expand Electric Bus Fleet
content: Everstone Capital-backed EV startup GreenCell Mobility has raised ₹330 Cr ($34.6 Mn) in an equity funding round led by Impact Fund Denmark to support the rollout of about 4,500 electric buses currently under deployment. The Mumbai-based startup is eyeing expanding its fleet to more than 5,000 e-buses across 105 cities across India. “Our focus is on executing our order book with rigour, strengthening service delivery and ensuring that the organisation keeps pace with the size and complexity of our operations. This equity investment gives us greater headroom to accelerate our plans while maintaining the standards of reliability, efficiency and customer experience that are fundamental to our business,” GreenCell Mobility managing director and chief executive Devndra Chawla said. Founded in 2019, GreenCell Mobility focuses on deploying and operating electric buses for public transportation. It acquires electric buses via contract manufacturing arrangements with vendors and then deploys them for both intercity and intracity travel. Backed by Eversource Capital, a joint venture between Everstone Capital and Lightsource, GreenCell primarily operates under the brand NueGo. It claims to operate more than 1,200 electric buses in India, including 900 on intra-city routes, 300 under its NueGo brand for inter-city travel, and 50 for MSRTC. The startup also runs over 270 charging stations to support its fleet. The startup previously raised $37 Mn from World Bank’s International Finance Corporation and also counts Eversource Capital, British International Investment and Tata Capital among its backers. India’s electric bus segment has so far drawn strong interest from development finance institutions and lenders backing vehicle deployments under long-term public transport contracts. GreenCell’s latest round suggested that investors are also beginning to back the operating platform layer in the category, not just asset financing. The investment highlights the role of institutional capital in expanding electric public transportation infrastructure in India. Large-scale electric bus deployments require funding not only for vehicles but also for the operational capabilities and charging infrastructure needed to support them. Earlier in March, electric bus manufacturer PMI Electro Mobility, along with its electric bus platform Allfleet, has signed a definitive agreement with private equity giant KKR for an investment commitment of up to $310 Mn, to help scale the electric bus platform and focus on expanding its presence across India. PMI subsequently filed for an IPO via the confidential route last month. The post GreenCell Mobility Raises ₹330 Cr To Expand Electric Bus Fleet appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Build, Buy, Or Rent? How Indian CTOs Are Rethinking The AI Stack
content: For Indian enterprises adopting AI, choosing the technology is only part of the challenge. Deciding what to own, how much to spend, and where AI can deliver measurable business value is becoming just as important. A December 2025 government backgrounder, citing Nasscom’s AI Adoption Index, said 87% of enterprises in India were actively using AI solutions . As adoption expands, technology leaders face a more complex choice: buy ready-made solutions, build capabilities in-house, or access models from external providers. Frontier models have made it easier to add AI capabilities to products and workflows. But the decisions around cost, speed, data, and business outcomes are increasingly intertwined. For enterprises and startups, the challenge is to identify which parts of the AI stack can create a lasting advantage and which to source externally as the technology evolves. These questions shaped the second roundtable held on the sidelines of Inc42’s inaugural CTO Summit 2026 , where technology leaders discussed how they are building AI-led systems and organisations. Moderated by Abhinav Johri, partner, technology consulting, EY India, the conversation brought together: Govind Soni, cofounder, CoinSwitch & Lemonn Harsh Sahu, cofounder and CTO, Matters.ai Kiran Reddy Singam, VP, product and tech, BigHaat Shanti Kuropati, founder, SeedlingLabs Shiv Buddharaju, VP, engineering, Oxmiq Labs Vikas Roy, director, engineering, Vahan.ai Vinay Rai, executive VP, technology, Netradyne Vivek Manoharan, CEO and CTO, Gravitas Building An Edge With Context And Workflows The conversation began with a question: as AI moves from experimentation into core business processes, does every problem require a new technology layer? Matters.ai’s Sahu argued that the starting point should be a deep understanding of the domain. Knowing where existing solutions fall short can help technology leaders build differentiated products. “I feel that founders and tech leaders need to know their specific domain really well to not only see the existing gaps but also use AI to fill in those gaps in a way that was never done before,” said Sahu. This emphasis on domain knowledge led to a distinction between the intelligence a company can source and the business context it develops itself. SeedlingLabs’ Kuropati argued that while frontier models change rapidly, proprietary data, context, and workflows can offer a more durable advantage. “If it is around data or context, you have to own it, irrespective of which frontier model you are working with, because that eventually becomes the moat for any AI-native founder, while the rest of the technology solutions remain largely the same,” said Kuropati. For CoinSwitch & Lemonn’s Soni, operational context matters most when accuracy directly affects customers’ money. “When you’re dealing with customer money, all operations become very critical, and accuracy can’t be compromised. So whenever you’re building something, that has to be built on top of that 10-year-old context, and not just with some new technology in isolation,” said Soni. What To Own, What To Rent Retaining control of context does not necessarily mean owning every technology layer around it. The discussion moved beyond the traditional build-versus-buy framework to examine what companies need to own, what they can rent, and how those choices change over time. Oxmiq Labs’ Buddharaju said these decisions span multiple dimensions, with one choice often affecting another. In AI, the workload involved in developing a product can also differ substantially from what it takes to serve customers at scale. “Technology choices are not simply about buy versus build. The real question is what you want to own, what you want to rent, and for how long. In AI, that distinction becomes even more important because the workload for building a product can be very different from the workload for serving customers,” said Buddharaju. Netradyne’s Rai made the case for renting intelligence. With frontier models evolving rapidly, he argued that building and maintaining an in-house model could leave companies playing catch-up. “Unless regulation requires us to run our own models, we are better off renting intelligence right now. The leaders keep changing, and an open-source model that is ahead today could leave you behind within weeks. For most companies, speed and flexibility matter more than owning the model itself,” said Rai. Making AI Economics A Product Decision Alongside ownership and flexibility, participants examined another test for AI deployment: its impact on business economics. BigHaat’s Singam said technology decisions must be tied directly to business metrics, with their contribution to margins assessed before deployment scales. “Whenever we deploy anything, we look at which metric it is moving and whether that change is positive or negative for our contribution margin. Whether it is fulfilment, RTOs, users or technology costs, we need to understand the economics before we scale,” said Singam. For Gravitas’ Manoharan, this assessment begins at the product development stage. A model’s ability to perform a task is only one consideration. The cost of running it also determines which features are viable. “Cost economics really matters to us, and it defines the product features we build. When we develop AI, we have to ask whether the economics will be sustainable within one or two years,” said Manoharan. He cited the example of converting US healthcare clinical charts into ICD and CPT codes. While AI models could produce useful outputs, the cost of processing each chart had to be weighed against the existing BPO-led process. This comparison makes unit economics an early filter for deciding which AI features to pursue. At Vahan.ai, Roy said AI expenditure is similarly linked to measurable productivity gains. The objective is to automate processes and increase the number of placements each telecaller could handle. “Clients care about outcomes, while we care about efficiency. For us, AI meant automating processes and asking which human decisions AI could handle. The real test was whether that could help us do more placements per telecaller,” said Roy. Across the roundtable, a common approach emerged: retain control of the context that differentiates the business, stay flexible on the models powering it, and assess the economics before scaling. For technology leaders navigating the next phase of AI adoption, these decisions will shape both the systems they build and the value they deliver. The post Build, Buy, Or Rent? How Indian CTOs Are Rethinking The AI Stack appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Urban Company Eyes Fresh Fundraise A Year After IPO As InstaHelp Losses Mount
content: Home services company Urban Company is considering a fresh fundraise a little over a year after its stock market debut in September 2025, amid continued spending on its instant household services vertical InstaHelp. The company’s board will meet on Friday (October 16) to consider raising funds through equity shares or securities convertible into equity shares, in one or more tranches, it said in an exchange filing. The routes under consideration include a preferential allotment, private placement, QIP, or another legally permissible mode, or a combination of these. Urban Company is also scheduled to release its Q2 FY27 numbers on the same day. The fundraise proposal comes as the company continues to invest in InstaHelp amid intensifying competition from Snabbit and Pronto. The vertical’s expansion weighed on Urban Company’s profitability in FY26 and remained a drag in Q1 FY27. InstaHelp Weighs On Profitability Urban Company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹235 Cr in FY26, compared with a net profit of ₹240 Cr in FY25, while operating revenue grew 34% YoY to ₹1,692 Cr. In Q1 FY27, operating revenue rose 44% YoY to ₹528 Cr, while its consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to ₹65 Cr from ₹98 Cr in the preceding quarter. Excluding InstaHelp, the company reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹67 Cr. InstaHelp’s revenue grew 26% QoQ to about ₹11 Cr, while its adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹132 Cr from ₹119 Cr in Q4 FY26. However, its adjusted EBITDA loss per order narrowed to ₹346 from ₹447 over the same period. Management has said spending on InstaHelp will remain elevated as the company seeks to strengthen its position in the category. During the Q1 FY27 earnings call, cofounder and CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal said the vertical would continue to require investment for at least the next two years. He also said InstaHelp was likely to remain a low-margin business compared with Urban Company’s core India consumer services operations. Management does not expect to make money from the vertical over the next five years and is working on the assumption that it will break even by FY31 . The proposed fundraise also comes while Urban Company retains a sizeable cash balance. It reported cash and treasury investments of ₹2,019 Cr as of June 30. Separately, ₹310.83 Cr of the ₹472 Cr raised through its IPO’s fresh issue remained unutilised at the end of Q1 FY27. The proceeds were allocated towards technology and cloud infrastructure, office lease payments, marketing, general corporate purposes, and issue expenses. Post-IPO Fundraising Gathers Pace Urban Company’s proposed fundraise comes at a time when publicly listed new-age tech companies are increasingly tapping equity fundraise opportunities , especially QIPs, to fund further growth soon after their IPOs. QIPs allow listed companies to offer equity shares or convertible securities directly to institutional investors like mutual funds, banks, and insurance companies. For instance, Kissht parent OnEMI Technology Solutions received shareholder approval to raise up to ₹832 Cr through a preferential issue, around four months after raising approximately ₹926 Cr through its IPO. Meanwhile, Swiggy raised ₹10,000 Cr through a QIP in December 2025, around a year after its stock market debut. Ola Electric raised ₹780 Cr through a QIP in June 2026, while Ather Energy raised ₹1,300 Cr through a QIP roughly 14 months after its IPO. Zaggle, RateGain, Nazara have also tapped institutional investors through QIPs. Travel tech company ixigo raised around $146 Mn through a preferential issue roughly 16 months after its listing. Ola Electric is now raising a further ₹1,000 Cr via rights issue that is set to open on October 22 for and close on October 30 at an issue price of ₹27 per share. title: Clueso Bags $10 Mn To Automate Enterprise Video Creation With AI Agents
content: AI video startup Clueso has raised $10 Mn (about ₹95 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Dharana Capital. The round also saw participation from new investors Founders Future and Neotribe Ventures, alongside existing backers Y Combinator and F7 Ventures. With the latest round, Clueso has raised a total funding of about $12 Mn to date. The startup last raised $1.4 Mn in a seed funding round led by F7 Ventures . Clueso plans to deploy the fresh capital towards expanding its enterprise sales and marketing operations and developing the AI agents powering its platform. It will also improve its video editing capabilities and deepen integrations with systems that store product and company information. Automating Enterprise Video Production Founded in 2023 by IIT Madras batchmates Akash Anand, Prajwal Prakash, and Neel Balar, Clueso helps businesses create and update videos using AI agents. The startup says its platform identifies gaps in existing video content, captures software workflows, and generates videos with scripts, voiceovers, animations, and captions. Users can edit these videos through a browser-based editor and refresh them when products, processes, or brand guidelines change. To support this, Clueso integrates with business tools to access company information and keep video content consistent. Its Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration also enables AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT to create, edit, and manage videos on the platform. “We position ourselves as a dedicated end-to-end platform for enterprises and not a single prompt-to-video tool that consumers or creators use,” Anand told Inc42. Clueso charges a subscription fee based on the volume of videos created and updated, the number of teams using the platform, and the products covered. The startup claims to have over 1,000 paying customers globally, including Atlassian, GitLab, Zendesk, Gainsight, Global Partners, Seismic, and Ironclad. Its Indian customers include PhonePe, Zoho, and MoEngage. According to Clueso, about 65% of its customers are based in the US, 20% in Europe, and around 10-15% in India. More than 70% of the videos created on the platform are customer-facing, including product launch videos and educational content. Other uses include employee training, onboarding, and compliance. Headquartered in San Francisco, Clueso has a 39-member team, including around 35 employees in India, with a significant presence in Bengaluru. Over the next 12-18 months, the startup plans to expand its enterprise integrations and customer base while automating more of the video production process. It also aims to track viewer engagement and use that data to improve video content. Anand said the long-term goal is to turn video into “a living system rather than a one-time asset you produce and forget about”. title: How DailyObjects Is Charging Up To The ₹400 Cr Revenue Mark?
content: Do you remember the first smartphone you bought around 2012? Chances are, you spent more time choosing the phone than thinking about its case. Phone cases were largely an afterthought, sold by local stores and small sellers in an unorganised market dominated by inexpensive, China-sourced products and copies of established brands. That began to change as smartphone adoption accelerated. Indians were increasingly willing to spend ₹20,000, ₹30,000, ₹40,000 and even ₹50,000 on their phones. As these phones became more central to everyday life, consumers began looking beyond basic protection, even demanding accessories that reflected their personal style — an opportunity DailyObjects tapped into early on. Founded by Pankaj Garg, in 2012, as a multi-category online business, the company narrowed its focus to smartphone cases in 2014. Over time, it expanded into bags, charging products and workspace accessories, building its brand around design and quality. Today, DailyObjects revenue crossed ₹200 Cr in FY26 , nearly doubling year-on-year. It is targeting ₹400 Cr in FY27 while working towards EBITDA profitability. But the more interesting part of DailyObjects’ story is not just how quickly it is growing today. It is how long it took to build a brand in a category that many consumers once barely thought about. Making Phone Cases More Than A Commodity DailyObjects had started as a multi-category online business, but by 2014, it decided to focus on smartphone cases. Rather than spread its resources across different product lines, the startup chose to focus on one category, differentiate through design and quality, and build a customer base willing to pay a premium. The category offered an opportunity to build a design-led brand in a market crowded with inexpensive, unbranded products. Consumers could walk into almost any mobile shop and find a case, while copies of products from established international brands were also widely available. DailyObjects’ answer was to make the product itself more distinctive. The startup began offering designer cases and collaborating with artists, bringing design into a category largely treated as a commodity. But differentiation was not limited to aesthetics. DailyObjects also wanted its products to compete with global brands on quality and materials. But building a better product was only half the battle. DailyObjects also had to decide how it wanted to grow. The startup had begun as a multi-category business, but it chose to drop car accessories and other retail products to concentrate on smartphone cases, which it saw as a larger and faster-growing opportunity. The idea was to build depth in one category before expanding into others. The same thinking shaped its distribution strategy. DailyObjects could have leaned on marketplaces to reach a wider audience and chase volumes. Instead, it largely stuck to its own channels, believing marketplaces could help sell a product but could not build a brand for it, even though it was a slower, more demanding route. The startup had to generate its own traffic, establish a distinct design identity and convince consumers to pay more for products they could find at a fraction of the price elsewhere. During this period, the startup raised ₹9 Cr from Ronnie Screwvala’s Unilazer Ventures . But according to Garg, the business had an important advantage: it had been profitable from its early stages. That gave it the room to grow without relying heavily on deep discounts or chasing marketplace volumes simply to keep the business running. DailyObjects stayed focused on phone cases for nearly five years before entering another major category. Its approach was to establish a foothold in one category, build distribution around it and then move to the next. By resisting the rush to scale through marketplaces, DailyObjects had more time to build a direct relationship with its customers. That strategy continues to define the business today, with nearly 70% of its sales coming through its own channels. DailyObjects’ Playbook: Making Everyday Products Desirable There was a logic to what DailyObjects added next. The startup was not looking to build a sprawling catalogue of accessories. It wanted to find products that appealed to the same customer it had won over with phone cases. The idea took DailyObjects into bags in FY21, opening up a much bigger opportunity than phone cases. However, it also brought a new challenge: manufacturers were unwilling to take on its small orders. Therefore, DailyObjects decided to make bags itself. The operation began with just two tables and eventually grew into its own factory. Today, bags account for around 40-45% of the company’s revenue. They are manufactured entirely in India at its own facility, which employs around 600 people. DailyObjects’ average order value is now around ₹26,000 and has been rising about 10% every year. The startup attributes the increase to products such as bags, power banks, and premium phone cases. Two years later, in FY23, DailyObjects entered into charging products. It was during this time that the startup bagged $10 Mn from 360 One Asset for product innovation and expanding its manufacturing capabilities. Its charging and STAC categories have grown nearly threefold since. The latest example is NODE, a modular wireless charging system around consumers carrying several devices between home, work and travel. The startup currently has around 50 core SKUs, excluding colour and size variants. Its revenue has grown from ₹ 24.1 Cr in FY21 to ₹39.2 Cr in FY22, to ₹84.4 Cr in FY24 and ₹110 Cr in FY25 . Garg said that the startup closed FY26 at over ₹200 Cr. While the founder didn’t divulge bottomline details for FY26, DailyObjects posted a loss of ₹16 Cr in FY25. The startup is yet to file its FY26 audited financials with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. The Next Challenge: Taking The Brand Beyond Metros DailyObjects spent years building its own traffic and customer base, a slower process that gave it greater control over how its products were presented and how they were priced. The payoff is beginning to show in its customer metrics. The company says its lifetime repeat purchase rate stands at around 45%. Its average order value has also risen by roughly 10% YoY to about ₹2,600, suggesting that customers are increasingly spending across its wider product range. Its customer base has also moved beyond the metros. Around 35–40% of DailyObjects’ sales now come from Tier III and IV cities, while another 20–25% comes from Tier II markets. The shift points to a broader opportunity: consumers in smaller cities are increasingly willing to spend on products that combine design with everyday utility. DailyObjects is now expanding its reach into cities such as Vizag, Patna, Ludhiana, Indore, Lucknow and Surat. But reaching more customers is only one part of the next phase. The other is making that growth more profitable. DailyObjects is currently operating close to break-even and remains on track to achieve EBITDA profitability in FY27. It expects operating margins, currently around 5%, to expand to 15-20% over the next four to five years. The improvement is expected to come from a combination of factors, including a higher-value product mix, a larger contribution from offline retail and greater supply-chain efficiencies. Recently, D2C lifestyle startup DailyObjects has raised ₹332 Cr ($34.3 Mn) in a Series C funding round co-led by Xponentia Capital Partners, Anicut Capital and Axiom Asia Private Capital. The funds will allow DailyObjects to scale its offline network, deepen its product and R&D capabilities, strengthen brand building and evaluate opportunities in international markets. DailyObjects’ Offline Push Comes With A Bigger Test For years, DailyObjects’ biggest asset was something consumers could not touch: the brand itself. Now, it is bringing that proposition into physical stores. The startup currently operates 13 exclusive brand outlets. It is opening two to three stores a month and plans to add 30-35 stores in FY27. Over the next five years, it aims to build a network of 150-160 stores. It is also present at 300 Apple premium reseller outlets. For DailyObjects, this is more than a conventional D2C brand moving offline. It is a chance to put the products at the centre of the buying experience. Consumers may discover them online, but a physical store lets them feel the materials, examine the finish and understand how a product works before paying a premium for it. According to the founder, all stores become profitable from the first month of operations. Its airport stores, in particular, are generating margins of close to 15% from the first month. Rather than limiting itself to India’s largest cities, DailyObjects is using physical retail to reach markets where it already sees significant online demand. It is also beginning to explore international markets. The startup is researching the US, where it already receives around 1,000 orders a month without dedicated marketing. But as the business grows, so will the challenge. With DailyObjects targeting ₹400 Cr in revenue in FY27, can it scale its offline and international presence while building a profitable business without losing what made its brand distinctive? title: The Quick Commerce Code: Breaking Playbooks Of Brands Winning The 10-Min Delivery Game
content: India’s quick commerce story is no longer about convenience. What started as a channel for forgotten groceries and last-minute essentials is now reshaping how Indians shop, consume and expect to receive products. With India’s quick commerce market projected to become a $40 Bn opportunity by 2030 and platform GMV expected to cross $68 Bn by 2031, instant delivery is evolving from being an optional consumer convenience into a core retail channel. The scale of this transformation is already visible. Blinkit reported a GOV of ₹13,300 Cr in Q3 FY26 , while Swiggy Instamart clocked ₹7,938 Cr during the same period. Together with Zepto, these platforms now operate more than 4,300 dark stores across the country, fundamentally changing how products are discovered, purchased and consumed. For consumer brands, this momentum has far-reaching implications. Categories such as beauty, personal care, packaged foods, beverages, baby care, wellness and household essentials are witnessing growing demand through high-intent purchases completed within minutes. At the same time, a new generation of D2C brands is using quick commerce for more than distribution. They use it to acquire customers, test demand, and drive growth. Meanwhile, as consumer behaviour shifts, brands must rethink how they operate. Brands are redesigning product portfolios around immediacy. Packaging formats are evolving for smaller baskets and impulse purchases. Demand forecasting, inventory allocation and replenishment cycles are becoming significantly more dynamic as businesses adapt to an always-on consumption environment. Yet, success in the channel requires much more — a series of decisions around assortment, pricing, inventory, fulfilment, visibility and platform strategy. Against this backdrop, Inc42, in collaboration with Nitro Commerce , is launching “ The Quick Commerce Code” — a five-part series that explores how consumer brands are building, adapting, and scaling within India’s rapidly expanding 10-minute economy. Through conversations with founders and operators, the series will look beyond headline growth metrics to understand what works on the ground. From customer acquisition and assortment strategy to operational execution and profitability, the series will examine the playbooks shaping the next phase of consumer commerce in India. Here’s What To Expect The Quick Commerce Code series will spotlight a diverse set of consumer brands navigating India’s rapidly evolving instant commerce ecosystem. From customer acquisition and category creation to inventory management and profitability, each brand offers a different lens into what it takes to win in the 10-minute economy. “With The Quick Commerce Code series, we want to decode how the next generation of D2C and FMCG founders are building businesses around real-time intelligence, rather than fragmented data. The winners will be those who can connect inventory, margins and platform dynamics into a single decision layer and act on it quickly,” said Umair Mohammed, founder and CEO of Nitro Commerce. The series will be packed with crucial insights from Zodiac, an autonomous AI copilot designed to help D2C and FMCG brands manage and scale their business across quick commerce platforms, giving visibility into inventory, sales, competitor pricing, share of shelf and ad performance. Notably, Nitro Commerce acquired Zodiac in March this year. Here’s a sneak peek at some of the brand stories coming up in the series: How Fix My Curls Is Turning Quick Commerce Into A Discovery Engine For Fix My Curls, quick commerce has evolved from a fulfilment channel into a powerful customer acquisition and discovery engine. The brand uses affordable SKUs to drive product trials, unlock demand from new consumer cohorts and adapt its portfolio for impulse-led purchases. The article will decode how Fix My Curls is using quick commerce to expand beyond its core audience and build a stronger top-of-funnel engine. PeeSafe: How To Build Demand In An Emerging Category PeeSafe’s quick commerce journey highlights how instant delivery can become a powerful lever for category creation. The company has used the channel not only to improve accessibility but also to drive awareness, encourage repeat purchases and expand demand across its portfolio. In an interview with the cofounder of PeeSafe, Rithish Kumar, we will break down how the brand is navigating evolving consumer behaviour while building one of India’s leading women’s wellness brands. Gramiyaa’s Game Plan For Quick Commerce’s Toughest Arena Operating in the highly competitive food and staples segment, Gramiyaa offers an insider look at the realities of building a quick-commerce-led business. The company has focused on a concentrated SKU portfolio, prioritised stock availability, and navigated the operational complexities of scaling in quick commerce. In this article, we will talk about the economics, inventory challenges and execution playbook behind Gramiyaa’s growth journey. Decoding The New Rules Of Consumer Commerce The Quick Commerce Code documents how consumer brands are adapting to the biggest shifts underway in India’s commerce ecosystem. Curated for founders, operators and investors, the series goes beyond traditional growth narratives to uncover decisions that have the potential to directly impact brands’ growth metrics. On this, Mohammed of Nitro Commerce urged brands to move beyond chasing GMV or simply spending more on ads in their quick commerce endeavour. “They need to maintain high fill rates, connect ad spending to real-time inventory, automate routine decisions and optimise for contribution margin. The brands that get this right can scale the channel profitably while continuing to build their own D2C channels and long-term customer relationships,” Mohammed added. All in all, the highly anticipated series The Quick Commerce Code from Inc42 will tap into similar fundamentals (as Mohammed mentioned) to decode strategies, trade-offs, and operating playbooks for brands sparring in the 10-minute delivery war zone. title: Manufacturing Startup ThinkMetal Raises ₹27 Cr To Initiate Commercialisation
content: Manufacturing startup ThinkMetal has raised ₹27 Cr (around $2.8 Mn) in a funding round led by India Angel Network’s VC fund IAN Alpha Fund. Other investors, including deeptech focused VC 3i Partners, among others, also participated in the round. The fresh funding will help ThinkMetal in developing its product stack, expand the type of materials it utilises as well as strengthening its R&D capabilities. The Chennai-based metal additive manufacturing startup is also looking to fuel its hiring with the fresh capital. “This investment is an important step in ThinkMetal’s journey from technology development towards commercialisation. We’ll use this capital to strengthen our product development, expand our team and materials capabilities and accelerate adoption across industrial applications,” cofounder and CEO Sabyasachi Ghosh said. Founded in 2021 by Ghosh and Arushi Sharma (CTO), ThinkMetal is a Chennai-based metal additive manufacturing startup that builds industrial printing systems that can manufacture tools such as moulds, dies, jigs and fixtures. Its SistemT1 machine uses metal fused additive manufacturing to build components layer by layer from wound metal feedstock. The process is followed by debinding and sintering to achieve the required strength. The hardware works alongside the startup’s proprietary FuseX materials and Thinkware software. ThinkMetal claims its system can produce metal parts up to 10X faster and at half the cost of conventional manufacturing methods. Its customers include Ants Ceramics, ZeQube Technologies and Hosur CNC, while its components serve applications across the automotive, aerospace and defence sectors. Prior to this round, ThinkMetal raised around $1.1 Mn from YourNest Venture Capital to scale production of its first-generation system. The startup operates in India’s additive manufacturing market, which is projected to grow from $677.4 Mn in 2023 to $3.75 Bn by 2030. The funding comes at a time when the need for deeptech-focus manufacturing firms is rapidly escalating, with the sector attracting a significant interest from institutional investors in recent times. As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals, a 2.8X jump from $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025 . Hence, startups in the deeptech manufacturing domain are emerging and also getting significant traction from VCs. For instance, Ethereal Machines recently raised $28.5 Mn in its Series B funding round led by Avataar Ventures to build a 3 Lakh sq ft mega-factory near Bengaluru. Similarly, companies like Fledgetec System also develop custom-built components, assemblies, and engineering solutions for the aerospace, defence, industrial, and specialised technology sectors. title: Speciality Chemicals Startup NuSynth Raises ₹36.5 Cr From Avaana Capital, Shastra VC
content: Bengaluru-based NuSynth Technologies has raised ₹36.5 Cr (about $4 Mn) in a seed funding round co-led by Avaana Capital and Shastra VC. The startup will use the fresh capital to strengthen its R&D and technology capabilities, develop an initial portfolio of proprietary chemical processes, build scale-up capabilities, and expand its team. Founded in 2026 by Poorvank Purohit, Ramesha A R, Abhishek Deo and Dipak Bajaj, NuSynth combines chemical R&D with AI to develop alternative processes for making complex chemicals, initially focusing on pharmaceuticals and electronics chemicals. The startup aims to address challenges associated with conventional chemical synthesis, including complex, multi-step processes, high material and energy costs, dependence on imported intermediates, and the use of hazardous reagents. To address these challenges, NuSynth re-evaluates starting materials, reaction pathways, and process economics. According to Avaana Capital, its processes seek to reduce reaction steps, eliminate hazardous reagents, lower temperature requirements, and replace solvent-intensive processes with catalytic and water-based alternatives. NuSynth follows an asset-light manufacturing model, working with Indian manufacturing partners to translate its laboratory research into industrial-scale production, the investor said. Supporting this work is an R&D platform that combines predictive synthesis models with an AI-enabled engine. The startup said the engine converts experimental data from each R&D cycle into a proprietary knowledge base to accelerate future molecule selection, experimentation, and commercial scale-up. “At NuSynth, we are going back to first principles – questioning established routes, redesigning processes and engineering them for commercial scale from day one. Our ambition is to build proprietary processes from India that can deliver superior economics and sustainability, and serve customers across global markets,” Purohit said. India has built considerable capacity in chemical manufacturing but developing proprietary synthesis processes could help companies address dependencies on imported intermediates and improve manufacturing economics. NuSynth joins a clutch of startups combining R&D with manufacturing partnerships in the speciality chemicals segment. Investors have previously backed startups like Distil, Scimplify, and Mstack to develop chemical solutions and expand their reach in global markets. The funding also comes at a time when India’s deeptech sector continues to draw investor attention across industrial and manufacturing innovation themes. Indian deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals in Q3 2026, a 176% increase from $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. This outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn. title: DealShare CEO Kamaldeep Singh Steps Down Amid Acquisition Talks
content: Amid a potential fire sale on the horizon, ecommerce unicorn DealShare’s CEO Kamaldeep Singh has stepped down from his role to join electric mobility solutions provider Indofast Energy as its CEO. Singh took to LinkedIn to make the announcement but didn’t specify the reason behind his exit. Singh had joined DealShare in December 2022 as its president, before transitioning to the role of CEO in January 2024 to spearhead the struggling startup as it revives its value-commerce business. He had a near 15 year long stint with Big Bazaar prior to DealShare, where he served as the CEO for more than a year. “After more than 25 years of building and transforming consumer businesses, I am stepping into an industry that is itself going through a fundamental transformation. Mobility is being reimagined. I believe the winners in this transformation will be those who put customer experience at the core and technology at the backbone,” Singh said. For context, Indofast Energy operates a fast charging battery-as-a-service network for EVs across India. It is a joint venture between Indian Oil Corporation and SUN Mobility. The company is planning to invest over $1 Bn over the next three years to deploy more than 10,000 battery-swapping stations across 50-plus cities. Singh intends to lead Indofast Energy’s next phase of growth, accelerating business expansion, strengthening its market presence and building a scalable and sustainable energy and mobility ecosystem across India. What This Exit Means For DealShare The exit comes about a month after Inc42 reported that Singh was serving his notice period, while CFO Ashish Shah was also looking to exit the startup. As of now, the ecommerce startup is yet to announce its replacement. The CEO exit comes amid ongoing questions around DealShare’s business model and future ownership. The startup’s founding team — Sourjyendu Medda, Vineet Rao, Sankar Bora and Rajat Shikhar — all exited by 2024. DealShare, which is known for online grocery delivery catering to middle and lower income “Bharat” households in tier-II and tier-III cities, has seen mounting competition pressure in the ecommerce landscape. DealShare began scaling back its online operations in April 2026 and eventually stopped fulfilling orders from its warehouses, effectively shutting down its two-hour delivery model. While the app remains available, its online business has dwindled to “next to zero”, Inc42 reported in September. The startup continues to operate physical stores, although further offline expansion has been put on hold. Amid all this, the startup is now reportedly in advanced discussions with online pharmacy Truemeds for a potential acquisition through a share-swap transaction that could value DealShare at just over $90 Mn, a 95% drop from its peak unicorn valuation. Westbridge is a common investor in both startups, holding roughly 18.4% of DealShare. Notably, the transaction is yet to materialise, with Truemeds’ existing investors not necessarily aligned with the deal. DealShare is also in talks with other potential buyers, according to sources Inc42 spoke to earlier. It has raised nearly $400 Mn to date from investors such as WestBridge Capital, Z47, Tiger Global, and Alpha Wave Global. It reached a peak valuation of $1.7 Bn in 2022. On the financial front, DealShare’s revenue from operations fell to 13.3% YoY₹432.4 Cr in FY25 from ₹499 Cr in FY24, while its net loss narrowed 91% to ₹87.7 Cr from ₹167.7 Cr. title: FSSAI Eyes Tighter Quick Commerce Rules For Expiry Dates, Food Labelling
content: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is considering dedicated regulations for ecommerce platforms, including quick commerce players, and cloud kitchens to tighten food safety compliance and product disclosures. The proposed rules would require online food listings to display manufacturing and expiry dates and batch numbers, and hold platforms accountable for misleading claims made by manufacturers, Bloomberg reported. The regulator is also considering mandatory disclosure of cloud kitchen photographs and addresses FSSAI CEO Rajit Punhani told ET that the regulator has held consultations with ecommerce and quick commerce companies and started inspecting dark stores and cloud kitchens. “We’re planning to amend the regulation so that consumers know the manufacturing date, expiry date and batch number of products they’re ordering,” he said. The regulator is also considering stricter checks on dark store storage conditions, including the handling of frozen products, as per the Bloomberg report. The proposed changes come amid increased scrutiny of quick commerce platforms such as Blinkit, Zepto, and Swiggy Instamart over their failure to display essential product information, including expiry, best-before and use-by dates. While platforms often mention a product’s shelf life, consumers may not know its actual expiry date or batch number before placing an order. The proposed ecommerce rules are part of the FSSAI’s broader crackdown on food safety and labelling violations . Prosecutions involving ecommerce companies have risen at least five- to sixfold over the past year, Punhani said, adding that platforms were improving compliance but not at the expected pace. Wider Food Safety Crackdown The scrutiny extends to food manufacturers and their labelling practices. The FSSAI has issued notices to more than 150 food and beverage makers, including Nestle, PepsiCo, Dabur, ITC, Ferrero, Danone, Red Bull, and Abbott, over allegedly incorrect or misleading ingredient claims and other labelling violations. “We are doing nothing wrong; we are just implementing the regulations,” Punhani said, adding that large companies should lead by example and avoid misleading claims and advertisements. Alongside action over existing labelling requirements, the FSSAI is pursuing front-of-pack warning labels for packaged foods. The regulator proposed red, hexagonal labels displaying the amounts of nutrients such as sugar, salt, and saturated fat in an affidavit filed with the Supreme Court. Separately, PepsiCo, Reliance Consumer Products, and Monster Beverage have challenged the FSSAI notices in court. The companies recently secured procedural relief after a court found that they had not been given adequate opportunity to respond or present their cases to the regulator. Punhani expressed confidence in the FSSAI’s position, telling Bloomberg, “They are resisting but we are far stronger and we have consumer support.” The regulator is also scrutinising supplements and nutraceuticals sold online. It is reviewing approvals granted three to five years ago to determine whether companies are making claims beyond those cleared by it. It plans to issue notices and suspend licences where it finds violations. The post FSSAI Eyes Tighter Quick Commerce Rules For Expiry Dates, Food Labelling appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Fundamentum Frontier Advisors Marks First Close Of ₹3,000 Cr Deeptech-Focused Fund
content: Ex-Fundamentum’s cofounder Ashish Kumar’s VC firm Fundamentum Frontier Advisors (F2A) has marked the first close of its growth-stage AI and deeptech fund at ₹3,000 Cr, India’s largest fund in the sector. Additionally, F2A said its LPs have approved plans to increase the size of the fund to ₹3,500 Cr, given the investor demand beyond the current capacity. The fund has raised capital from both domestic and overseas investors and will divide the funds across two vehicles. It plans to deploy the corpus into 12-15 companies over the next 2-3 years, writing cheques in the range of ₹100-200 Cr each. It claims to be in the advanced stages of closing three investments within the upcoming quarter. “More Indian companies are now building deeptech products for global markets, with India as their engineering and commercial base. Having worked with such companies from their early years, I have seen how much the right capital matters once the technology is validated and customers start to scale. We believe that is the stage at which F2A can help them become category leaders,” said general partner Debraj Banerjee. F2A was founded by Fundamentum Partnership partner and cofounder Ashish Kumar earlier this year . Kumar, Banerjee and Vivek Singla are F2A’s general partners while Fundamentum’s former general partner Nandan Nilekani is the anchor investor for the fund. The VC investor’s strategy focuses on three sectors: consumer business leveraging AI and frontier technologies, enterprise software, deeptech infrastructure and engineered systems. It targets India-domiciled companies earning revenue from India as well as globally. Despite the common involvement of team members including Kumar and Nilekani between Fundamentum and F2A, the two are separate legal entities. Notably, Fundamentum has itself launched its new fund this year – its third fund with a target corpus of ₹2,200 Cr. Deeptech is the latest investor darling as funding for the sector nearly tripled to $290 Mn across 28 deals in the quarter ending September 2026, as against $105 Mn across 29 deals a year ago, per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’ report. The likes of South Korean gaming giant KRAFTON , global VC investor Accel , and Mumbai-based early-stage VC AUM Ventures have all mentioned plans to bet on this space in the past few months.
