title: NPCI Defers UPI MDR Implementation Till Post Diwali
content: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has deferred the introduction of merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions until immediately after Diwali, pushing back the October 15 rollout. The NPCI said its UPI and Services Steering Committee took the decision keeping the festive season in mind. The revised implementation date will be notified separately. The announcement confirms a delay in the rollout but does not set January 1, 2027, as the new deadline, as earlier reports had suggested. Under the proposed framework UPI MDR, merchants would be charged an MDR of 0.40% on eligible P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 per transaction. The move had faced significant push back from retail traders’ associations. The committee was also reportedly considering exempting businesses with an annual turnover of up to ₹40 Lakh from the proposed fee. The new framework marks a shift from the zero-MDR regime. Transactions up to ₹2,000, person-to-person (P2P) transfers and eligible small-merchant transactions would remain exempt. The All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) and the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) had called for a ‘No UPI Day’ on October 2 to protest the proposed charges . They withdrew the planned protest after meeting Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on September 30. AIMRA had sought a fixed, nominal charge for digital transactions instead of the proposed 0.40% MDR. The AICPDF, meanwhile, has estimated that the fee could add ₹7,000 Cr-₹9,000 Cr in annual costs across the FMCG distribution and retail ecosystem. Recently, the Supreme Court refused to stay the Centre’s implementation of MDR charges on select UPI transactions. However, it directed the Centre and other respondents to file their counter-affidavits within four weeks, observing that the issue was “less legal and more technical”. UPI Monetisation And The Cost Of Payments Earlier this month, NPCI MD and CEO Dilip Asbe defended the proposed MDR framework, saying a market-driven economic model for UPI is necessary to fund rising cybersecurity, scalability and infrastructure costs. Asbe said banks and payment companies would need to invest continuously in AI to strengthen security and maintain user trust. “The ability and the tools with the hackers are really very powerful compared to what we could actually use inside,” he said, adding that AI was expensive to deploy and would require sustained investment to protect payment systems. Meanwhile, UPI continued to see double-digit year-on-year (YoY) growth in volume and value last month, despite a marginal month-on-month (MoM) decline. UPI processed 24.07 Bn transactions worth ₹29.37 Lakh Cr in September , down 1.8% and 1.5%, respectively, from 24.51 Bn transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August. On a YoY basis, transaction volume grew 23%, while transaction value rose 18%. Average daily transactions increased to 802 Mn in September from 791 Mn in August, while the average daily transaction value climbed to ₹97,913 Cr from ₹96,205 Cr. title: e-Sprinto Enters B2C Market With G1 Escooter, Eyes 5,000 Sales By March
content: Electric two-wheeler maker e-Sprinto has entered the business-to-consumer (B2C) market with the launch of its G1 family electric scooter, priced at ₹89,999 onwards, as the startup looks to expand beyond its business-to-business (B2B) fleet operations. The G1 is available in three variants priced at ₹89,999, ₹94,999 and ₹99,999, respectively, with all prices ex-showroom Delhi. The variants offer battery options of 2 kWh, 2.5 kWh and 3 kWh, with claimed ranges of up to 80 km, 100 km and 130 km on a single charge, respectively. The scooter features three riding modes, Eco, City and Sport, with maximum speeds of 30 kmph, 40 kmph and 50 kmph, respectively. Developed over nearly two years of research and development, the G1 has been designed for families and everyday commuters, the startup said. Customer deliveries are scheduled to begin from January 1, 2027. e-Sprinto is targeting sales of around 5,000 G1 units by March 2027, cofounders Atul Gupta and Shalu Gupta told Inc42. The launch comes amid a broader push by electric two-wheeler makers to tap the family scooter segment, traditionally dominated by petrol-powered scooters. While Ather Energy has its family-focused Rizta range, Simple Energy entered the segment with its Wave scooter in 2026, priced from ₹1.09 lakh. Ola Electric, meanwhile, has expanded its S1 portfolio across price points, including scooters below the ₹1 Lakh price point. The trend points to EV makers looking beyond performance-led models and early adopters to reach households and everyday commuters, making affordability, comfort, storage, reliability and after-sales service key areas of competition. From Fleet Operations To Consumer Mobility Founded in 2022 by Vinod Gupta, Atul Gupta, and Shalu Gupta, e-Sprinto has built its business around electric two-wheelers for commercial and fleet customers. The startup says it has more than 70,000 vehicles on Indian roads, supported by three manufacturing facilities with a combined annual production capacity of 1.5 Lakh units. Its B2B customer ecosystem includes mobility and fleet operators such as Zypp Electric, Hala Mobility, Ride EV, Bike Bazaar, Shadowfax, among others. The startup also works with delivery and quick commerce businesses through its partners. e-Sprinto’s B2C foray comes following a 1,564% month-on-month jump in its monthly escooter registrations to 1,997 units in September, according to Vahan data. The cofounders attributed the growth partly to festive demand and the commissioning of a third manufacturing facility in July, which doubled production capacity and helped the startup fulfill pending orders. The cofounders claimed that the startup typically sells twice as many scooters as are recorded on the Vahan portal, as its portfolio also includes low-speed scooters that do not require registration. According to the cofounders, e-Sprinto’s vehicles deployed in commercial operations have an uptime of over 97%. They said operating in demanding fleet environments has helped the startup understand vehicle reliability, servicing requirements, and performance across geographies. The G1 differs from its fleet-oriented products in both battery configuration and vehicle design. While e-Sprinto’s B2B scooters use swappable batteries, the G1 has a fixed battery, larger 12-inch tyres, and seating designed for families. The cofounders said the B2C foray aims to diversify the startup’s customer base and reduce its dependence on fleet demand. While commercial customers drive volumes, the dealership network will help it reach individual buyers. However, dealer margins and the cost of building a retail network could weigh on profitability initially. The cofounders expect unit economics to improve with higher sales volumes and plan to use the startup’s existing manufacturing and service capabilities to support the expansion. They said e-Sprinto is bootstrapped and EBITDA profitable, with no plans to raise external capital in the near term. The startup expects its revenue to double YoY in FY27 but didn’t give its FY26 revenue number. It is also targeting a double-digit EBITDA margin. Dealership Expansion & Growth Plans To support its B2C push, e-Sprinto plans to add around 10 dealers a month, targeting approximately 150 dealerships by FY28. These will be standalone outlets, with expansion initially focused on northern India, followed by western and southern markets. The startup plans to enter eastern India in a later phase. It will fund the expansion through internal accruals and promoter capital. Alongside the dealership rollout, e-Sprinto is investing in R&D and hiring more employees. Its workforce has grown from around 10 in its first year to approximately 260, according to the cofounders. The expansion comes amid growth in India’s E2W market. Registrations rose 12.2% MoM to 2.07 Lakh units in September , with TVS and Bajaj together accounting for half the market. The sector has also attracted investor funding in recent months . In Q3 2026, River raised $120 Mn, Yulu secured $93 Mn, and Ultraviolette raised $85 Mn. title: Why AI Agents Are Forcing Enterprises To Rebuild Their Data Foundations
content: Enterprises have spent years accumulating data. Making it usable for AI is proving harder. Systems built for different teams, functions, and use cases have left information scattered across databases, applications, and workflows. For AI systems expected to reason across an organisation, having data somewhere is not enough. They need to find it, understand what it means, and use it in the right context. The gap is becoming visible as Indian businesses move AI from pilots to production. According to a Dun & Bradstreet survey , 73% of surveyed Indian businesses report some measurable returns from AI investments, but only 4% say their enterprise data is fully ready to support AI at scale. Closing this readiness gap means addressing years of accumulated data debt. Customer identities may be fragmented across systems, operational data may remain siloed, and information organised for reporting may not meet the needs of AI systems expected to retrieve it and act on it. Bringing this scattered information together is only the first step. To make it usable for AI, enterprises must determine which data needs to be available in real time, how agents will understand its context, and what permissions should govern access. These decisions also shape the infrastructure and models needed to serve each use case, influencing whether the value of deploying AI justifies its cost. How enterprises should approach these decisions was the focus of “Building The Data Foundation For AI At Scale” , a roundtable hosted by Inc42 in partnership with Oracle at its CTO Summit 2026 . The roundtable featured: Abhimanyu Saxena, cofounder, InterviewBit & Scaler Dhruv Gupta, cofounder, Orchard Healthcare Himanshu Garg, CTO, Kapture CX Naveen Dachuri, CTO, Yulu Palanivel Saravanan, head of infrastructure cloud engineering, Oracle Priyanka Nahata, founder, CodeKarma Technologies Syed Mohd Bilal, head of data science, Perfios Vinay Murthy, senior director of product, Zeta Moderated by Alexy Thomas, partner, technology consulting, EY India, the discussion examined how business needs should guide data architecture, agent access, and deployment costs. Outcomes Before Architecture For Orchard Healthcare’s Gupta, the starting point is the problem the business wants to solve. That means working backwards from the intended outcome, rather than adopting a technology and searching for a use case. “The way we think about it is backwards. What is the problem to be solved?” Gupta said his team followed this approach when building its customer data platform. The six-month project began only after the team established how it could improve customer understanding, retention, and the wider business. Perfios’ Bilal echoed this emphasis on defining the outcome before choosing the tools. “Start from an outcome focus and then figure out what to build rather than, you know, thinking about tools first.” Agreeing on an outcome, however, still leaves enterprises with an architectural choice: build for that specific use case or invest in a platform that supports multiple applications. Bilal outlined the trade-off: use-case-led development addresses immediate needs, while a platform-first approach provides a broader foundation for future applications. Zeta’s Murthy argued that AI is making the broader platform harder to ignore. As employees and systems begin creating agents, companies may struggle to anticipate every use case or the data each agent will require. “What AI gets in is that the use cases are no longer in your control,” Murthy said. This unpredictability puts greater demands on the underlying platform. It must serve known applications while allowing new agents to find and interpret data for needs the enterprise has yet to define. Building Context Into Data Supporting these new uses requires more than a database connection. An agent must understand how the information is organised, what it means, and how to retrieve it efficiently. Oracle’s Palanivel pointed to information spread across databases such as Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and MongoDB, as well as unstructured knowledge. Connecting an agent directly to these systems introduces another challenge — it may not understand the database schema or generate queries that the database can handle efficiently. The layer between the agent and the data therefore needs to interpret its structure and meaning and plan how to retrieve information. Palanivel explained that traditional systems relied on humans to connect operational data with business decisions. For autonomous agents, some of that reasoning needs to be encoded into the data layer itself, making a semantic layer increasingly important. “The semantic layer is only required or is becoming mandatory to support the reasoning for the agent,” he said. Beyond helping agents interpret information, semantics can also make retrieval more focused. Perfios’ Bilal suggested that it can narrow the information an AI model needs to search through, helping it retrieve relevant data. Creating this context requires input from people who understand the data. Bilal argued that those working closest to it are best placed to define its meaning, and that understanding should be consistent across tools and platforms. But making information understandable does not mean every agent should be able to use it. Enterprises also need boundaries around whose data an agent can access and for what purpose. Governing Agent Access InterviewBit & Scaler’s Saxena illustrated this challenge with a question — if a model learns from Bank A’s data, can that knowledge be used for Bank B? Using enterprise data to train or improve AI systems, he pointed out, carries both legal and technical implications. Similar questions arise within an organisation when employees use AI tools to work with business information. Kapture CX’s Garg argued that organisations cannot realistically prevent employees from using frontier models, making controls around that usage critical. “So how do you build governance around this right? That is the most critical thing,” he said. For Kapture, this means applying access controls to the knowledge and context graphs its agents use. Alongside these controls, Garg said the company is building agent harnesses to automate testing and evaluation. Making The Economics Work Permissions and testing address how agents operate, but enterprises must also establish whether each deployment delivers enough value to justify its running costs. Yulu’s Dachuri distinguished between internal AI tools, where companies can set budgets, and AI embedded in customer-facing products, where usage and costs are harder to predict. For Yulu’s bike-repair use case, the calculation is more measurable. The company can weigh reductions in manual touchpoints and turnaround time against the cost of deploying AI. “So the value versus cost balance. It is most important,” he said. Keeping this balance in check also requires choosing models suited to the task. Kapture, for instance, is using smaller models for predictable tasks, such as order-status queries, rather than relying on frontier models for every interaction. Oracle’s Palanivel noted that organisations are moving away from a one-size-fits-all frontier-model approach, with open-weight models offering a more predictable cost structure for some workloads. The choice of model, then, sits alongside the data and governance decisions that determine whether AI can work reliably in production. Enterprises need to provide relevant context, enforce access controls, and evaluate agent behaviour, while keeping infrastructure and model costs aligned with business value. For businesses already seeing returns from early AI projects, scaling those gains means getting these elements to work together. The foundation must support both the use cases they can define today and the demands that new agents will place on their data. title: Winter Wear Steps Into The Rental Zone
content: With winter almost here, it’s almost time to reopen those trunks and suitcases holding the family’s woolen and warm clothes. The sweaters, shawls and jackets go through trials before being rolled out for the season. This is a familiar routine for anyone who lives in a city or town with a winter to speak of, and every season brings the same challenges of keeping up with the trends and the changing needs of everyone in the family. For everyday wear, keeping an old favourite sweater or cardigan makes sense, but going on a holiday or dressing up for an occasion in winter changes things. Plus, if you live in Mumbai or Chennai or any other temperate city with no real cold months, buying winter wear for that occasional trip to the mountains or cold cities means spending on things you will barely touch once you’re back home. Take a casual look at the online aisles of winter wear on Myntra or AJIO or any fashion platform. The total expense adds up rather quickly and grows quite large when the whole family needs new winter clothes. For instance, Decathlon lists a snow jacket somewhere at ₹5,999 and a winter parka at ₹6,999. And those are some of the less pricey options out there when it comes to gear that keeps you warm in true cold. Beyond the price, there’s the responsibility of cleaning, storing and maintaining it until the next use. For many, this is simply not worth the hassle. So can rental change the game? Mumbai-based winter apparel and thermo-layer brand Kosha is offering winter wear rentals with a good number of options starting at ₹990 for seven days. Bengaluru’s SharePal is renting a wide assortment of products at rates as low as ₹50 per day, while Mumbai-based Roamwear has packaged winter wear into its travel wardrobe rental for women. Rentals are not a new idea in India. We touched upon the circular fashion economy earlier and Gen Z’s interest in thrifting and value-conscious shopping is being seen in winter wardrobes too. Just like in wedding wear and designer fashion earlier. Unsurprisingly, the market for winter rentals is quite large in markets where winter travel is a major tourist attraction. But players such as Finland-based Winterent, Sweden’s SkiStar, Austria’s SkiGala and Japan’s Soranoshita offer outdoor winter clothing near ski retreats. These largely target tourists and not individuals in the region. That’s the key difference between these players and the Indian startups we spoke to. In India, winter wear rental is undoubtedly an experiment. The question is: is the market big enough for the startups to scale? Where’s The Ceiling? Rishav Jain, managing director, Alvarez & Marsal India, says the idea of creating a shared economy matters more than which category is being targeted. Anything with a high average selling price and low usage can move into the rental or shared economy game, especially in a market like India. Kosha founder Yuktie Jhangiani Verma believes that traction is inevitable even though the category is small today. “This is a brand new space. It is still too early to define its absolute ceiling, the growth momentum is undeniable. Exciting shifts are happening across consumer behaviour every single month,” she added. One of the key differences between renting and direct sales is that the former targets premium products that are not widely available or are out of reach of individuals due to their price. This is why rental for winter wear as a business is positioned and linked with travel. Startups are targeting customers that are booking ski trips, treks or their next European winter holiday. This makes rental a small add-on cost to the overall travel budget. “Fashion renting works when the item costs above roughly ₹6,000-8,000 and you expect two or fewer trips. Rental typically prices at 10-20% of retail per rental period, so a ₹10,000 jacket at ₹1,490 a week is a clear saving, compared to another jacket that sells for ₹3,299, where that rental price will be 45% of directly buying one. In the latter case, most customers would prefer to buy the jacket than rent it,” TDV Partners’ founder and managing partner Ujwal Sutaria said. For instance, a published comparison by Indiahikes’ Crosstrek says renting a full set of trekking gear comes up to ₹2,435 for six days, compared to ₹18,250 for buying that same gear. This includes trekking shoes, a padded jacket, rain jacket, backpack and accessories. These are indicative prices rather than what a typical customer might end up spending if they take their time researching the options in the market but not everyone has the time for that. Sutaria said that as more and more Indians make international trips, the market for rentals is growing. India reported 32.71 Mn overseas departures in 2025, and Japan alone went from 233K to 315K+ Indian visitors between 2024 and 2025. The market for Indian tourists to Northern European destinations like Sweden, Iceland and Norway has grown tremendously in the past two years. “Viable categories are heavy parkas, ski and snow suits, snow boots and trek gear. Frequency is the ceiling, because by the third trip the customer buys,” he added. But purely depending on customers planning travel can end up becoming a paradox for rental platforms. More travel plans means more rental opportunities, but it means customers are also more likely to purchase rather than rent every time. Which is why rental platforms cannot just market the affordability; it’s also about keeping up with the latest styles, materials and trends. Even a short weekend trip can be a window for rental platforms. Some are targeting customers that change their wardrobe with the destination rather than using their existing winter wardrobe. “When you rent, you have the flexibility of a changing wardrobe with every itinerary. You get a sleek trench for a city break, a technical parka for sub-zero trips, and a vibrant ski jacket for the slopes, all at a fraction of the retail cost,” Kosha’s Verma told Inc42. Small factors like holiday photographs and social media posts influence choices too. Customers who want a different look on each trip may keep renting even when they can afford to buy. The stigma around rented clothing is disappearing fast among metro users. So what can brands do in this space to scale? According to Sutaria, customer experience and discovery are the critical levers here. Distribution also matters because the category is sensitive to other parts of the economy i.e. travel. Founders in this space added that resale of retired rental stock is a second revenue line but that requires a captive audience base as well. The next demand signal is therefore whether customers return for another itinerary, and whether those orders extend beyond the same short travel season. And that dictates the whole economic model for rental platforms. Going Beyond The Rental Season Once the holiday is over and the heavy winter coat comes back to the platform, the startup has to prepare it for another paying customer. So maintenance and upkeep is a central challenge and can skew unit economics. Any company in this space has to provide for reverse pickup without which the rental proposition does not work. The dry cleaning and storage is managed by platforms to limit the exposure to costs and to maintain high quality of products. At Kosha, Verma said, clothes go through a 10-point checklist before being rented out again. So the key metric here would be rentals-per-SKU. The margins are baked into the rental fee, so the actual growth should be seen in the number of rentals for every jacket, coat or sweater in the inventory. This is just like the RentoMojo or Furlenco business model, and it’s a parallel for which we have numbers too. As per recently listed RentoMojo’s disclosures , the company had 8.51 Lakh items as of March 2026, of which 83.34% were out on rent. Items purchased nearly ten years ago had already earned 5.12X their original cost by this point in time. More than 56% of the assets added in 2017 and 60.92% of those added in 2018 were still generating revenue in FY26. These are metrics that even rental platforms have to track, and the shelf life of a wool sweater may be much shorter than that of a hardwood table or other items that Rentomojo offers on rent. In other words, the business for fashion rental platforms — which includes winter wear — depends on how much of the stock is out on rent, how long each item lasts and how much it costs to put it back into circulation. For winter wear, the peak demand sits in a short travel season, so the share of stock out on rent across the full year is also another number to watch when assessing startups and their operations. As of now, none of the companies we have spoken to have hit the kind of scale to speak meaningfully about these metrics and their revenue in detail. That itself gives us a clue as to how winter wear startups are still figuring their way around the economic models of this business. Perhaps the end of this winter season may give us an idea of where this is headed. SPOTLIGHT | HOW UPLIANCE.AI IS MAKING HOME COOKING SMARTER Bengaluru-based Upliance.ai builds AI-powered kitchen appliances designed to simplify everyday cooking. Its flagship device automates chopping, stirring, grinding and heating through a smart jar, built-in weighing scale and touchscreen-guided recipes. The appliance offers more than 750 guided recipes across 34 cuisines, covering everything from Indian curries and biryanis to pasta, soups and desserts. Users follow step-by-step instructions on the screen, while the device manages cooking temperature, timing and stirring. Upliance.ai is expanding beyond its cooking assistant into smart air fryers powered by its UpAI technology. The fryers let users turn food photos, recipe reels and YouTube recipes into cooking settings. The startup reports more than 6.6 Lakh meal sessions since November 2022 and sales crossing 7,500. THE DEEP DIVE ECOMMERCE BUZZ Nat Habit Raises ₹142 Cr : The personal care brand’s Series C round was led by Trident Growth Partners, with existing investors participating. Nat Habit plans to expand its retail network tenfold to two lakh stores, enter modern trade, strengthen quick commerce and launch sunscreens and serums. Bewakoof’s FY26 Net Loss Jumps 19% : The D2C fashion brand’s operating revenue grew 40.6% YoY to ₹243.1 Cr in FY26, while net loss widened from ₹73.2 Cr. title: Toothsi Parent MakeO Raises ₹90 Cr For India, Southeast Asia Expansion
content: MakeO, the parent of clear aligner brand Toothsi, has raised ₹90 Cr (about $9.4 Mn) in a funding round led by Singularity AMC, with participation from DSP family office, Genesis, and Unispace Ventures. The Mumbai-based startup will use the fresh capital to expand its offline presence across India and Southeast Asia and strengthen its manufacturing operations. It will also invest in consumer experience, clinical centres, and backend technology. MakeO is also evaluating acquisitions of dental and aligner businesses across India and Southeast Asia as part of its offline expansion The fundraise follows its acquisition of Singapore-headquartered Zenyum, which expanded its presence across Southeast Asia. MakeO had announced an agreement to acquire Zenyum in February. In 2025, it also acquired Apple Dental for ₹10.9 Cr in a cash-and-stock deal . The chain operates 20 clinics across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, extending MakeO’s offline presence beyond major Indian cities. Following the Zenyum acquisition, the combined group has a network of around 1,100 partner dentists across 10 countries. It also operates more than 60 offline clinical centres and has served over 4 Lakh consumers, according to the startup. Founded in 2018 by Arpi Mehta, Pravin Shetty, Manjul Jain and Anirudh Kal, makeO initially offered teeth aligners under the brand toothsi. In 2022, it merged its brands toothsi and skinnsi under makeO to offer dental, skin and hair treatments on one platform. MakeO had raised over $100 Mn before the latest round from investors including Eight Roads Ventures, 360 ONE Asset, and Paramark Ventures. Its earlier fundraises include ₹100 Cr in June last year and a $16 Mn round led by 360 ONE Asset and the investment office of Ashish Kacholia in January 2024. MakeO said its combined business has crossed ₹500 Cr in revenue and turned EBITDA profitable earlier this year. It aims to double revenue over the next two to three years. The startup’s expansion plans come amid projected growth in India’s clear aligner market. According to Market Research Future, the market is projected to grow from $466.99 Mn in 2025 to $2.83 Bn by 2035, at a CAGR of 19.74%. title: Visibility In The AI Age, Zetwerk’s IPO & More
content: Dominating The AI Shelf Space Thirty years after the internet’s first ad banner went live, digital marketing is undergoing its biggest transformation yet. As users swap search engines for AI chatbots, the rules of brand discovery and consumer engagement are being rewritten. Ads In AI Era: Rather than typing keywords into Google and navigating links, consumers are now using AI tools for product recommendations. This behavioural pivot has given rise to answer engine optimisation and generative engine optimisation. But unlike legacy SEO systems, AI platforms offer no common ranking system or standard playbook. Attribution Problem: For marketers, the biggest challenge is determining whether AI visibility actually drives traffic, customers and sales. This is because multi-step queries and zero-click answers make traditional click attribution nearly impossible. Inconsistent citations and reliance on third-party content further weaken brand control. As such, experts believe that brands should build a consistent information flow across their digital ecosystem to avoid appearing next to misinformation or unsuitable content. Ads Enter The Chat: As marketers struggle with the AI RoI question, OpenAI is also creating a new commercial layer around its AI assistants. It has begun rolling out ads for ChatGPT’s free and Go users in India, with more than 50 brands expected in the initial rollout. By tapping ad agencies and opening a self-serve ads manager, OpenAI is looking to monetise its huge user base in the country. The New Toolkit: Meanwhile, a new wave of startups is building tools to bring measurement and commerce to AI search. While the likes of RankinLLM are tracking brand mentions and sentiment, TruCommerce is connecting product catalogues directly to AI platforms to enable in-chat purchasing. Then, there is also Gushwork that helps small businesses create content optimised for AI tools. As chatbots compress the path from discovery to decision, can brands solve the challenges around visibility, attribution, measurement and control? Let’s find out… From The Editor’s Desk Zetwerk Gears Up For IPO The B2B manufacturing startup’s public issue will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19. It has also set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share for its IPO, which will value the company at ₹25,583 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. The ₹5,012 Cr public issue will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS of up to 14.45 Cr shares, worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end. This comes a couple of months after Zetwerk filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in August. Separately, defence tech company Tonbo Imaging has also set a price band of ₹665-₹700 per share for its upcoming IPO, which will also open on October 15. The ₹852.1 Cr public issue will consist solely of an OFS component of up to 1.22 Cr equity shares. Tessolve Bags $75 Mn The semiconductor startup has raised ₹718 Cr in a round led by Vector Line Capital to fuel acquisitions, broaden its service offerings and strengthen its international business. It is also already in talks to close multiple acquisitions over the next couple of quarters. Founded in 2004, Tessolve designs AI chips and provides end-to-end engineering services across chip architecture, validation and testing. Hero Electronix acquired a controlling stake in the company in 2016. It has raised $265 Mn to date. The fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in the Indian deeptech sector, which is being driven by regulatory push, subsidies, a pivot to IP-driven products and a growing talent pool. The sector raised $290 Mn in Q3 2026 , up 176% YoY. PharmEasy’s FY26 Show The online pharmacy’s parent API Holdings managed to slash its net losses by 67% YoY to ₹520 Cr in FY26. This came as operating revenue rose 12.7% YoY to ₹6,618.5 Cr, driven by higher margins, capacity utilisation and fewer discounts. Giving a breakdown, the company said that its B2B businesses generated ₹4,082.4 Cr in revenue in FY26 with an EBITDA loss of ₹3.6 Cr. On the other hand, the B2C arm generated ₹1,334.5 Cr in revenue and reported an EBITDA loss of ₹44.1 Cr in FY26. Meanwhile, expenses also continued to bite. API Holdings’ consolidated expenditure stood at ₹7,146.7 Cr in FY26, albeit down 0.9% YoY. Purchases of stock-in-trade remained its biggest cost centre at ₹5,244.8 Cr, up 10.9% YoY. Top-Level Rejig At Nazara Founder Nitish Mittersain is stepping down as the MD of the gaming giant after a 27 year-long stint. CFO Rakesh Shah has also resigned to pursue external opportunities. Shah will be replaced by ex-Ness Digital Engineering executive Arun Agrawal. CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti has also been elevated to the role of executive whole-time director role for a period of five years. Meanwhile, Rohit Sharma has stepped down from the post of whole-time director. The reshuffle comes as much is happening at Nazara. Last month, Raymond Stauffer took over as the new CEO of the gaming giant. Nazara also de-subsidiarised its esports arm NODWIN Gaming earlier this year even as losses continue to pile up. The RDI Boost For Deeptechs The government has announced the first cohort of 19 second-level fund managers to deploy ₹7,131 Cr from the RDI fund. Fourteen AIFs and five focused research organisations have been selected to channel the capital to the eligible startups. The fund managers are also expected to mobilise capital equivalent to the RDI Fund’s contribution, expanding the pool of financing available for research-led startups. The Centre also plans to onboard additional fund managers going forward. Launched in November 2025, the RDI Scheme has an outlay of ₹1 Lakh Cr and aims to address the funding gap faced by startups developing high-impact technologies. Earlier this year, the fund had also allocated ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies. Inc42 Markets Inc42 Startup Spotlight Can Nextup Make Muscle Recovery Less Pricey? For people dealing with post-workout soreness, recovery tools can be difficult to choose. While many cheaper gadgets lack useful features, premium devices can stretch the budget. Nextup is plugging this gap with Pulse, which combines practical features with an accessible price point. Going Mass-Premium: Founded in 2024, Nextup is positioning itself between budget recovery gadgets and higher-priced products. Its flagship massage gun Pulse, features a 30W copper motor, a top speed of up to 4,200 RPM, four interchangeable massage heads and a 3,000mAh battery. Nextup claims that Pulse is quiet and operates at under 45 dB. The In-House Edge: The bootstrapped startup leverages a D2C-led model, selling through its own website and marketplaces such as Amazon. It also runs an in-house assembly facility, which gives it more control over quality and lets the team make product changes based on consumer feedback. It competes with the likes of Cult, Dr Physio and Agaro. Road Ahead: Going forward, the D2C brand plans to scale Pulse across online channels and build its creator community to spur repeat demand. It has also set its eyes on launching additional products as it expands from recovery into personal wellness and broader consumer electronics. So, can Nextup build a mass-premium wellness brand for Indians? Infographic Of The Day Sixteen Indian entrepreneurs earned a combined ₹43.4 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26. Even founders of loss-making Meesho, Swiggy and Ather took home crores in paycheques. Here is all about it… The post Visibility In The AI Age, Zetwerk’s IPO & More appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Hero Electronix-Owned Tessolve Secures $75 Mn To Expand Semiconductor Capabilities
content: Hero Electronix-owned Tessolve Semiconductor raised $75 Mn (₹718 Cr) in a funding round led by Vector Line Capital, with additional participation from existing backers TPG and Novo Tellus Capital Partners. The fresh capital will support acquisitions that complement its existing capabilities, broaden its service offerings and strengthen its international business. The company is already in advanced discussions to close multiple acquisitions over the next couple of quarters. It last acquired Germany’s Dream Chip Technologies GmbH (DCT) in a ₹400 Cr deal back in November 2024. “This investment will support acquisitions that further strengthen our offerings, and Vector Line’s focus on the sector and their relationships will add significant value,” Tessolve cofounder and chief executive Srini Chinamilli said. Founded in 2004 by Chinamilli, P Raja Manickam and Veerappan V, Tessolve provides end-to-end semiconductor engineering services, spanning chip architecture and design, validation, testing and embedded systems. The company is designing AI and HPC chips by leveraging its in-house pre-engineered semiconductor platforms and design flows to shorten development cycles, alongside a global lab infrastructure and partnerships with leading foundries, IP, EDA and test equipment companies. Tessolve claims to have worked with leading hyperscalers and 18 of the world’s top 20 semiconductor companies. Hero Electronix, the electronics and tech arm of Hero Group, acquired a controlling stake in the semiconductor company in 2016, with plans to complete a phased acquisition of a significant majority holding by the end of that year. “Two decades ago we started with silicon test engineering. Today we are designing and productising complete chips for the companies building AI infrastructure,” Chinamilli said. Tessolve last raised $150 Mn in a fresh round in 2025, led by TPG Growth. With the latest infusion, the startup’s cumulative funding stands at $265 Mn. The development comes amid broader momentum in India’s deeptech sector, where semiconductor and chip design startups have drawn rising investor interest. This increasing investor interest is also supported by the government’s ₹1.25 Lakh Cr India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, which was launched with an aim to build the country’s chip design and manufacturing ecosystem. Some examples of this include AI-native semiconductor verification startup VerifAIX’s $5 Mn seed funding round in September, HrdWyr $13 Mn Series A funding round , among others. Broader investor interest for advanced hardware and tech startups in India, which includes robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% YoY to $290 Mn, as per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026 . title: [Update] Alpha Wave Ventures Sells Lenskart Shares Worth ₹1,705 Cr
content: Update | October 12, 20:00 IST Lenskart early backer Alpha Wave Ventures has sold 2.64 Cr shares in a bulk deal valuing the stock at ₹645.31 apiece. The investor raked in ₹1,704.8 Cr via the stake sale today. The details of the buyers couldn’t be immediately discerned. Update| October 12, 17:48 IST Shares of Lenskart ended today’s trading session 4.4% lower at ₹647.95 apiece on the BSE. Its market capitalisation stood at ₹1,12,698.3 Cr ($11.7 Bn) at the end of the day. The bearish momentum of the stock came after reports of early investor A lpha Wave Ventures stake sale surfaced. As per reports, the VC firm plans to sell up to 1.6% of its stake in Lenskart for as much as ₹1,691 Cr, with the offer priced at a floor of ₹640 per share. The floor price is at a 5.6% discount to the stock’s closing price of ₹677.65 on October 9. The proposed sale comprises 15.1 Mn shares, or a 0.9% stake, with an option to sell another 11.3 Mn shares, equivalent to 0.7%. If the investor sells the full 26.4 Mn shares on offer, its holding in Lenskart will fall to 1.82% from 3.42%. The latest move adds to a series of stake sales by Lenskart’s early investors in recent months, with Alpha Wave itself having sold shares worth ₹1,856.8 Cr in August. Early Investors Continue To Pare Holdings In August, Alpha Wave Ventures sold 2.94 Cr Lenskart shares through multiple block deals at ₹630 apiece, according to NSE data. The transaction fetched the investor ₹1,856.8 Cr. The shares were picked up by a mix of institutional investors, including the National Pension System (NPS) Trust, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, Bajaj Life Insurance, HDFC Life Insurance, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and Kuwait Investment Authority. Alpha Wave Ventures held 3.42% of Lenskart, or around 5.9 Cr shares, at the end of June 2026. Its August sale reduced its holding by nearly 1.7 percentage points. The proposed transaction comes amid a broader round of stake sales by investors in the company. SoftBank sold Lenskart shares worth ₹2,887.9 Cr, while Temasek offloaded a 2.05% stake for ₹1,934 Cr last month. Earlier, in June, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority sold 4 Cr Lenskart shares in a block deal worth ₹1,960 Cr. An extended bull run for the stock has provided a fertile ground for investors to cash in. The company’s stock has zoomed over 48% on a year-to-date basis on the back of robust financial performance of the stock. On the financial front, Lenskart reported a 273% YoY surge in consolidated net profit to ₹228.4 Cr in Q1 FY27, up from ₹61.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, profit rose 12% from ₹203.6 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue grew 43% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹2,714.2 Cr. Including other income of ₹68.5 Cr, Lenskart’s total income stood at ₹2,782.7 Cr for the quarter. title: BYJU’S Parent To Hold 32% Stake In Aakash After Settlement: Report
content: Think & Learn Pvt Ltd (TLPL), the insolvent parent of BYJU’s, is set to hold around 32% in Aakash Educational Services once a settlement resolving its long-running shareholding dispute with the coaching company is fully implemented. According to an ET report, the stake will be higher than the roughly 25.75% TLPL held before Aakash’s ₹240 Cr rights issue became the subject of litigation last year. TLPL’s recorded shareholding fell sharply after Aakash withheld a portion of the shares it had subscribed for. The settlement will include allotment of rights issue shares as well as transfer of existing shares to TLPL, the report said, adding that there would be no cash consideration for the deal between TLPL, Aakash, and the coaching institute’s investor Manipal Group. Aakash and Manipal Group declined to comment on Inc42’s queries regarding the development. This comes a month after the Bengaluru bench of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) directed TLPL’s resolution professional (RP) and successful bidder Comprint Tech Solutions (India) to maintain status quo on assets auctioned by TLPL amid a dispute over their ownership. The Tribunal’s order followed claims by the RP of another BYJU’s group entity, BYJU’s K3 Education, that goods worth around ₹150 Cr had been auctioned for about ₹16 Cr. K3’s RP argued that the company had a substantial stake in the assets and that their further disposal could leave it without assets to continue its corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP). TLPL’s RP disputed the claim, arguing that TLPL had procured the hardware and owned the educational content stored on the devices. The NCLT observed that neither side had produced sufficient documentary evidence to conclusively establish ownership. The Tribunal directed Comprint to submit an inventory of the purchased assets, photographs and their storage address. TLPL’s RP was also asked to provide details of the assets, their valuation and the auction process. The NCLT has not cancelled the auction or made a final determination on ownership. The dispute stems from separate insolvency proceedings against TLPL and K3 Education. TLPL entered insolvency proceedings in July 2024 after the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) approached the tribunal over unpaid sponsorship dues of around ₹159 Cr. K3 Education is facing a separate insolvency process following a Section 9 petition filed by operational creditor Kritikal Solutions. Last month, Byju Raveendran reportedly proposed relinquishing his claimed beneficial interest in 17.89 Mn Aakash shares to settle Qatar Holding’s arbitration claim of over $235 Mn against him. The shares, held through Singapore-based Beeaar Investco Pte, represent about 5.7% of Aakash’s equity. They were acquired in 2022 using $150 Mn in financing extended by Qatar Holding, owned by the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), to Raveendran’s Singapore-based investment vehicle, BYJU’s Investments Pte Ltd (BIPL). Raveendran personally guaranteed the financing. Qatar Holding terminated the financing agreement after alleging defaults by BIPL and demanded more than $235 Mn, including early termination fees and penalties. It also alleged that the Aakash shares had been transferred to Beeaar, which it claims is beneficially owned by Raveendran, in violation of the agreement. The proposed settlement involving Aakash shares could affect the coaching company’s ownership structure and Qatar Holding’s recovery efforts. However, the settlement terms and the extent to which they would address the fund’s claims remain unclear. title: Zetwerk Sets IPO Price Band At ₹143-₹151 For ₹5,012 Cr Issue
content: B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk has set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share for its IPO, which will be worth ₹5,012.3 Cr at the upper end of the band. The issue comprises a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS of up to 14.45 Cr shares, worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end, according to its RHP. The IPO will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19. Anchor investor bidding will take place on October 14. At the upper end of the price band, Zetwerk is seeking a post-issue market capitalisation of around ₹25,583 Cr (about $2.7 Bn). The company has increased the fresh issue from ₹2,600 Cr outlined in its UDRHP. The OFS has also grown 49.2% from about 9.7 Cr shares. Promoters and cofounders Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan will each sell up to 1.42 Cr shares. Other selling shareholders include promoter group entity Creovate Innovation and funds associated with Peak XV Partners, Accel India, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Kae Capital. Zetwerk plans to use ₹2,160 Cr from the fresh issue to repay or prepay borrowings of the company and certain subsidiaries. The remaining net proceeds will fund acquisitions and general corporate purposes. Zetwerk filed its draft IPO papers confidentially in March, followed by its UDRHP in August . Inside Zetwerk’s Business Model Founded in 2018, Zetwerk operates a manufacturing platform serving businesses across industrial and consumer goods categories. It combines capacity from third-party suppliers and its own facilities to manage manufacturing orders across sectors including renewable energy, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil and gas, and industrial automation. Its customers include Siemens Gamesa, Acer India, boAt, NTPC Renewable Energy, CG Power and Industrial Solutions, and the Indian Air Force. As of June 30, Zetwerk operated 26 manufacturing facilities across India, the US, Germany, and Spain. It entered the unicorn club in 2021 after raising $150 Mn. It has raised over $900 Mn in funding to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, Greenoaks Capital Partners, and D1 Capital Partners. In July, Inc42 reported that Zetwerk had raised ₹500 Cr from Bharat Value Fund ahead of its IPO. Its RHP confirmed that shares worth ₹500 Cr were allotted to Bharat Value Fund and Bharat Value Fund – Series III on April 2. Revenue Grows, Losses Persist On the financial front, Zetwerk’s operating revenue increased 40.4% to ₹15,913.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹11,331.9 Cr in FY25. However, its net loss, including discontinued operations, widened to ₹1,606.2 Cr from ₹370.7 Cr. The FY26 loss included a ₹796.4 Cr exceptional charge linked to changes in share conversion ratios and a ₹453 Cr impairment charge in its discontinued civil infrastructure business. For Q1 FY27, operating revenue from continuing operations rose 55.4% to ₹4,117.9 Cr from ₹2,649.4 Cr in Q1 FY26. Its total net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr in the year-ago period. Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr came from discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included ₹803.2 Cr in exceptional charges from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business. Separately, Zetwerk and US-based transformer startup Ayr Energy reached a settlement in September , agreeing to withdraw pending claims in US and Indian courts and jointly seek termination of a related US International Trade Commission investigation. Zetwerk had accused Ayr Energy founder Anirudh Reddy, a former senior executive at the manufacturing platform, of misusing confidential information and trade secrets. Ayr Energy had filed counterclaims against Zetwerk, which disputed the allegations. Zetwerk’s IPO follows public market debuts of new-age tech companies like RentoMojo, Moneyview, Shiprocket, LEAP India, and ESDS Software this year. title: Tonbo Imaging Sets IPO Price Band At ₹665-₹700 For ₹852 Cr Issue
content: Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging India has set a price band of ₹665-₹700 per equity share for its ₹852.1 Cr OFS-only IPO. The IPO comprises an OFS of up to 1.22 Cr equity shares, with no fresh issue component. At the upper end of the price band, the IPO values the company at ₹4,009.8 Cr (about $480 Mn). The issue will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19, with anchor investor bidding scheduled for October 14. The selling shareholders include promoters and cofounders Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza, alongside investors such as CEAQ Technologies and Artiman Partners. The offer has been reduced from the 1.81 Cr shares proposed in its draft papers. SEBI issued its observations on its DRHP last month, after the company refiled the draft papers in August . Founded in 2003, Tonbo initially provided R&D and technology development services as a subsidiary of a research company. Following its buyout by the promoters in 2012, it shifted to manufacturing defence products, including advanced electro-optic and electronic systems. Currently, the company designs and develops defence electronics and imaging systems used for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting and other military applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, driver-vision systems, targeting equipment, fire-control systems and missile seekers. Tonbo is also developing newer defence products, including a loitering munition and a high-power microwave-based anti-drone system called WaveStrike. As of June 30, 2026, the startup had deployed more than 28,000 systems across 24 countries In April last year, Tonbo raised ₹175 Cr in a Series D funding round from investors including Florintree Advisors, Tenacity Ventures, and EXIM Bank at a reported valuation of ₹1,500 Cr. Tonbo follows an asset-light manufacturing model, outsourcing production to certified electronics manufacturing services partners such as Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology. Prototype development, system integration and qualification testing are undertaken in-house. On the financial front, Tonbo reported operating revenue of ₹36 Cr and a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. For the fiscal ended in March 2026, its revenue from operations declined 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr from ₹ 469.1 Cr in FY25. Net profit declined 43% YoY to ₹50.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹72.8 Cr in the previous year. title: Pledge, Sell, Pledge Again: Bhavish Agarwal & Ola Electric’s Dilemma
content: For close to two years, Bhavish Aggarwal has been stuck between a rock and a hard place. All to keep Ola Electric and his other ventures going without giving up control of the company he built. Between November 2024 and March 2025, Aggarwal pledged Ola Electric shares to raise debt for Krutrim Data Centre , the AI infrastructure and services company that he founded in 2023. Then in December 2025, he sold part of his stake in Ola Electric to repay the ₹260 Cr loan that covered the pledge and release the encumbered shares, selling 3.93% of his holding in the company. At the time, Ola Electric said repaying the loan meant the company should operate with zero pledge overhang. But ten months later, another pledge is here. On 30 September, Aggarwal pledged 20 Cr Ola Electric shares , or 4.32% of the company, against non-convertible debentures (NCDs) issued by Krutrim Data Centre. CTL Trusteeship holds the pledge on behalf of the debenture holders. Neither the filings nor Ola have disclosed how much Krutrim Data Centre is raising through these debentures. What is clear is that this is a bigger pledge than before — 20 Cr shares (4.32%) against 17.3 Cr shares (3.93%) that secured a ₹260 Cr loan in the previous instance. Ola Electric said that the pledge is solely meant to fund his subscription to the company’s upcoming ₹1,000 Cr rights issue, and that no shares are being sold, and that Aggarwal will invest on the same terms as every other shareholder Shriram Subramanian, founder of advisory firm InGovern Research, said that the EV firm scores poorly on what investors call the “say-do” ratio: how often a company does what it says. The situation around the pledges highlights this. He added that investors will read a founder pledging, clearing and pledging again as a sign of stress for the promoter or the promoter’s group entities, “and that may not be a good sign.” Especially after Ola raised ₹780 Cr through a qualified institutional placement (QIP) in June 2026. Four months later, it is asking shareholders for more. Ola Electric’s Cash Problem One thing we need to point out: Ola Electric’s rights issue is coming on the heels of the improved operating metrics. Market share rose from 5.1% in Q4 FY26 to 8.4% in Q1 FY27, but short of the 15–20% it targeted for 2026. But in the same quarter, rival Ather delivered 83,173 scooters, more than twice Ola’s 39,192, while posting a lower loss. Ola’s dealership rollout is still under way, and its gigafactory has not yet reached its 6 GWh target. Both are drags on its bottom line. In Q1 FY27, Ola Electric reported revenue of ₹455 Cr , down 45% from a year earlier and below its own guidance of ₹500–550 Cr. Its net loss narrowed to ₹336 Cr, the lowest in seven quarters, but free cash flow was still negative at about ₹351 Cr. At that rate, the ₹780 Cr raised in June covers roughly two quarters of cash burn. The rights issue, approved by the board on 28 September , would add up to ₹1,000 Cr. According to the draft letter of offer, about ₹350 Cr will go towards repaying or prepaying borrowings and ₹400 Cr towards organic growth. Of the money earmarked so far, nearly half goes to paying down debt. These are partly paid shares, which means investors pay in installments. The issue price, entitlement ratio and payment schedule are yet to be announced. The Idea Behind Pledging Instead Of Selling A rights issue is offered only to existing shareholders, in proportion to what they already own. Aggarwal still holds roughly 26.2% of Ola Electric shareholding. If he sits out this rights issue and does not buy in, his stake and therefore his control will shrink. According to the legal experts we spoke to, Agarwal also cannot simply borrow debt from Ola Electric. Section 67(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 bars a public company from giving financial assistance, directly or indirectly, through a loan, guarantee or security, for anyone to buy or subscribe to its own shares. Selling shares to invest in the rights issue would be counterproductive to Aggarwal’s goal of maintaining his stake in the company, so pledging shares is the only option on the table The money comes through Krutrim Data Centre, which, as a company, can issue debentures in a way an individual cannot. Aggarwal has used this route before , with the same company and the same kind of pledge. What has changed since is his priority. In December, he faced a similar choice and went the other way. With the stock near a record low at that time and his pledged shares closer to a margin call, he sold part of his stake to repay the loan and release the pledged shares. A margin call on pledged shares would have meant that Aggarwal would have had to deposit funds or securities to cover for the dropping market value of the pledged collateral. Aggarwal avoided this eventuality by selling a portion of his stake in December 2025, but now he is looking at pledging shares to protect his stake. For now at least, it would seem that retaining his control on Ola Electric matters more than any overhang from the pledge. The Krutrim Link The current shares pledged by Agarwal aim to secure debt on behalf of Krutrim Data Centre. That also puts a private company’s balance sheet directly behind a listed company’s shares. If, for instance, Krutrim Data Centre struggles to repay these NCDs, the pledged Ola Electric shares are exposed, and could be sold by the lender group, even if Ola Electric has recovered financially. InGovern Research’s Subramanian said that if Krutrim’s debt goes bad and the lender enforces the pledge, it could sell the shares, which would weigh on the stock. He called this an extreme scenario, but said the risk alone is an overhang: public investors will keep watching whether Krutrim is able to pay back the debt. But the lender has to give reasonable notice, sell, and return any surplus, and Aggarwal can redeem the shares until then. It is also not clear how the money raised by Krutrim reaches Agarwal, whether as a loan, an advance or in some other form, or whether all of it is meant for the rights issue. That route of funds transfer from Krutrim to Agarwal also matters, according to VPS Law Associates’s VP Singh. He says that under Section 185 of the Companies Act, a straight loan from Krutrim to Agarwal is not applicable, however it could be a likely scenario of Krutrim repaying some loan it already owes to Agarwal or Krutrim directly subscribing to Ola Electric rights issue through entitlements Aggarwal renounces in its favour. For Ola Electric itself, this would not be a related-party question. “A transaction only between Krutrim and Aggarwal does not automatically become an Ola Electric related-party transaction. That will kick in when Ola Electric or its subsidiaries deal with a related party,” Singh added. In the scenario that the lenders decided to enforce the pledge, Ola Electric’s board would have no say. “The shares are the promoter’s property and freely transferable; the company’s obligation is only confined to disclosure,” Singh said. Can Falling Stock Trigger A Crisis? A pledge is a loan secured by shares, and the value of that security moves with the stock price. That is exactly what makes it a double-edged arrangement. At around ₹37 a share, the 20 Cr pledged shares by Agarwal are worth roughly ₹740 Cr. Brokerages like Citi have set a target price of ₹26 for the next 12 months, indicating that investors should sell. Lenders in a pledge arrangement typically respond to a price fall by asking the borrower to pledge more shares. If the promoter cannot provide them, lenders can sell the pledged shares in the market. That is likely to result in a runaway effect where the price is pushed down further, triggering the call for more shares or more funds to cover the pledge. Subramanian elaborated, but he stressed that this is an extreme scenario. “If Ola’s stock keeps falling, the value of the pledged shares drops against the margin the lender requires. So more and more shares would have to be pledged. Either the promoter pledges more shares to hold the margin, or investors sell their shares to recover some money, which adds to the downward spiral,” Ola Electric’s investors have already seen a version of this. When Aggarwal sold shares in December to clear his earlier pledge, the stock fell 11% in two days and came close to its record low. Ola Electric’s stock has fallen about 30% over the past year and trades at less than half its IPO price of ₹76. While legally, there is no law that bars Agarwal from pledging the shares in a listed firm to secure debt for his private company, the cost he and Ola Electric pay is of credibility. The share entitlements to key shareholders and the schedule of funds payments will all be keenly watched out for. After that, the question is purely operational in nature. Ola needs to bring its quarterly cash burn down before the money from the QIP and the rights issue runs out. If Ola Electric needs to raise money again, Agarwal will face the same choice between selling and borrowing, and the cycle will begin anew. title: India’s Cleantech Funding Boom, The AI Safety Drill & More
content: EVs Power Cleantech Funding Boom India’s cleantech story accelerated in Q3 2026. The quarter saw the sector nearly triple its funding volume on the back of big-ticket electric mobility rounds and rising deal activity. So, what’s pulling investors towards the sector and can the momentum extend beyond EVs? The Cleantech Boom: As per Inc42 data, Indian cleantech startups raised a record $433 Mn in Q3 2026, nearly 3X from $118 Mn in the year-ago quarter. Although funding remained heavily concentrated in one segment, the sector’s broader momentum was evident: deal count rose 44% YoY to 23, while average cheque size zoomed to $19 Mn from $7 Mn in Q3 2025. The EV Concentration: Within cleantech, electric mobility dominated funding charts in Q3. Just three EV startups – River, Yulu and Ultraviolette – raised a combined $298 Mn, nearly 69% of the sector’s total haul in the quarter. The concentration highlights the sector’s over-dependence on a small group of well-funded ventures. Decoding The Boom: Cleantech funding surged as investors shifted their focus from climate narratives to commercially-viable businesses solving real problems. Electric mobility led the charge, supported by rising EV registrations, stronger consumer demand and improving PMF. What also helped was rising component localisation and growing investor confidence. The Road Ahead: Experts believe that the sector’s long-term outlook will depend on broadening investment beyond EVs to other emerging areas such as energy storage, grid tech and green hydrogen. They also see deeper localisation improving margins and reducing supply chain risks. As such, unit economics and a clear path to sustainable revenues will be a key focus area for backers going forward. As investor conviction expanded across the cleantech ecosystem in Q3, why did capital remain tightly locked within a handful of EV players? Let’s find out… From The Editor’s Desk The AI Safety Drill OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI giants are rehearsing how they would respond to a catastrophic incident involving AI. The companies are set to engage with US lawmakers as experts believe a major AI incident could happen within 12 months. The planning comes as AI companies look to avoid a serious failure, which could prompt sweeping public backlash, new restrictions and scrutiny of industry leaders. The fear is that a major AI incident could impact internet infrastructure or financial systems. The safety drill comes as LLMs find software vulnerabilities and coordinate agents. In the past few months, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported several instances, where their agents bypassed safeguards and accessed real-world infrastructure. Weekly Startup Funding Tanks Indian startups managed to raise a cumulative $123 Mn last week, down 47% from $234 Mn in the preceding week. However, deal count more than doubled week-on-week to 25. DailyObjects and Lumio emerged as the most funded startups last week. Ecommerce dominated the funding charts last week, raising $63.9 Mn across nine deals. Fintech ranked second with $24 Mn in funding, followed by advanced hardware and technology at $10 Mn. Early-stage funding trends remained strong as pre-seed and seed-stage startups collectively bagged $12.5 Mn across nine deals. 3one4 Capital and Fireside Ventures emerged as the most active investors, backing two startups each. Mixed Week For Startup Stocks Of the 66 new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage, 36 gained in the range of 0.1% to nearly 25% last week. The remaining 30 fell in the range of 0.23% to 13.93%. MobiKwik and PW emerged as the biggest gainers, while Yudiz and Zappfresh shed the most. The combined market capitalisation of 67 new-age tech stocks, including the recently listed AceVector, stood at $154.71 Bn at the end of last week compared to $153.61 Bn for 66 companies in the preceding week. Going forward, investors will be tracking inflation data, crude oil prices, progress in Iran-US negotiations and global bond yields for market cues next week. Nat Habit Bags ₹142 Cr The D2C personal care brand has raised around $14.7 Mn in its Series C round led by Trident Growth Partners to expand its distribution network, product portfolio and manufacturing capabilities. Founded in 2019, Nat Habit sells Ayurveda-based personal care products, including hair oils, masks, scrubs, and face creams. Having served 60 Lakh customers so far, the D2C brand currently claims to clocking ₹330 Cr in annualised gross revenue. The funding comes amid growing investor interest in the homegrown ayurvedic wellness segment, which is being driven by growing demand for traditional formulas, the rise of quick commerce, premiumisation and multi-functional products. India’s Listed Startup Tracker India is home to over 70 listed new-age tech companies, with a combined market capitalisation of $173 Bn. Of this, 18 startups went public in 2025 and another 15 have already crossed the milestone this year so far. Together, these listed startups boast a combined revenue of $26 Bn. A majority of these new-age tech companies, nearly 74%, are profitable, while the remaining posted a cumulative loss of $932 Mn in FY26. Delhi NCR is home to the largest number of listed startups. On the sectoral front, fintech and ecommerce account for the biggest chunk of listed new-age tech companies. Inc42 Markets Inc42 Startup Spotlight Turning Agri-Waste Into Steel Industry’s Next Big Power Bet India’s steel industry still runs largely on coal, while millions of tonnes of agricultural waste goes waste every year. Climitra is connecting these two problems by converting waste biomass into industrial-grade biochar, offering industries a route to carbon removal. Turning Waste Into Fuel: Founded in 2025, Climitra is building a vertically-integrated startup to convert biomass into bio-coal. It uses AI and geospatial intelligence to map and assess biomass availability, and then converts locally-sourced waste into fuel through a proprietary pyrolysis process. A Coal Substitute: Climitra’s bio-coal is designed as a 1:1 replacement for fossil coal in steel-making, reducing the need for costly furnace retrofits. The startup claims that its output contains 75-85% fixed carbon, has a gross calorific value of 6,500–8,000 kcal/kg and can cut emissions by up to 90% compared with fossil coal. Beyond Bio-Fuel: Climitra’s business model extends beyond bio-fuel. The startup is targeting both industrial decarbonisation and carbon removal, using its existing biomass supply chain. The startup claims it has already validated its bio-coal with Tata Steel, JSW Steel and AM/NS India. Backed by InfoEdge Ventures, the startup is eyeing a piece of the Indian biomass briquette market, which is projected to become a $2.1 Bn opportunity by 2032. So, can Climitra turn agricultural waste into a lower-carbon fuel for its steel industry? title: Qualcomm Sells Shadowfax Shares Worth ₹157 Cr In Bulk Deal
content: Early backer Qualcomm Ventures has sold 57.1 Lakh shares of listed logistics company Shadowfax via an open-market transaction for ₹157.3 Cr. According to BSE data, the chipmaker, via its affiliate Qualcomm Asia Pacific Pte Limited, sold the shares at ₹275.3 apiece to rake in the amount. This represented a discount of 6.6% against the stock’s last closing price on Monday. Qualcomm Asia Pacific Pte Ltd owned 2.26% stake, or 1.32 Cr shares, in Shadowfax at the end of June 2026. However, the chipmaker then diluted some of this shareholding and sold 75 Lakh shares worth ₹183.9 Cr in August. Qualcomm Ventures first invested in Shadowfax during the logistics company’s $22 Mn Series C round in 2018, alongside Mirae Asset and Eight Roads Ventures. This is the latest bulk deal involving Shadowfax in recent months. Since August, private equity (PE) giant TPG has offloaded Shadowfax shares worth more than ₹700 Cr across multiple bulk deals. The bulk deals come as investors look to book profits amid a sharp uptick in Shadowfax’s stock prices. Shares of the logistics company have surged 29.3% in the past three months, and are up more than 122.91% in the last six months. This jump has come on the back of healthy financial performance by the startup . The logistics major saw its consolidated net profit surge 8X to ₹65.4 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹8 Cr in the year ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 65% YoY and 10% QoQ to ₹1,358 Cr in the quarter under review. Following the results, Shadowfax also revised its FY27 revenue growth forecast to 38-40% , a significant jump from the 28-30% guidance projected just a quarter ago. Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Bansal and Vaibhav Khandelwal, Shadowfax operates a logistics network serving ecommerce, quick commerce and D2C brands. The company was listed on the stock exchanges earlier this year. It currently operates across more than 16,372 pincodes and plans to increase its network of dark stores from 47 to 100 by March 2027 as it looks to strengthen its quick commerce business. Shares of Shadowfax closed Monday’s trading session 0.12% lower at ₹294.75 on the BSE. The post Qualcomm Sells Shadowfax Shares Worth ₹157 Cr In Bulk Deal appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Nazara Top Deck Shuffle: Founder Mittersain Steps Down As MD; Caratlane’s Sacheti Takes Executive Role
content: Listed gaming major Nazara Technologies announced a major leadership reshuffle today, highlighted by founder Nitish Mittersain stepping down as the company’s managing director. Mittersain, who founded the company in 1999 and took it public in 2021, has assumed a new role as “Founder and Non-Executive Director”. He will continue to provide strategic guidance to the board. Meanwhile, CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti, who joined the board as an additional director earlier this year, has been elevated to an executive whole-time director role for a period of five years. Sacheti will now assume a new position to oversee strategic initiatives and take on some operational responsibilities. “He understands the consumer business space, digital consumer ecosystems … He brings extensive entrepreneurial,consumer and brand building experience,” the gaming major said in its disclosures to the bourses earlier today. Besides, the board also noted the resignation of Rohit Sharma as Whole-time Director, effective from January 1, 2027, onwards, as he decided to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities. Sharma joined the company’s board as an advisor in January 2025 and was later roped in as executive director in August. Additionally, Nazara’s CFO Rakesh Shah has also resigned to pursue external opportunities and will be replaced by Arun Agrawal, former global CFO at Ness Digital Engineering. Shah, who has been with the gaming major since 2010, will exit the company on October 15 though he will assist with transition duties for 90 days. The change at the top of Nazara’s hierarchy comes shortly after Mittersain exited as CEO amid a turning point in the listed company’s journey. Back in March, Nazara acquired a 50% stake in Spanish casual gaming studio Bluetile Games and its associate BestPlay Systems for a deal worth $100.3 Mn at base value, with performance-linked earn-outs of up to $98.2 Mn. However, the terms of the deal were later restructured such that Nazara acquired 100% of Bluetile and BestPlay for a fixed cash consideration of $303 Mn, shelling out $89 Mn upfront and committing to pay the remainder in agreed tranches by April 1, 2027. Besides, the gaming giant also approved a ₹733.5 Cr fundraise via preferential issue of equity shares to the founders and senior leadership team of Bluetile and BestPlay, including Bluetile’s founder and CEO Raymond Stauffer, who also took over from Mittersain as CEO on September 1. Notably, Bluetile and BestPlay together generated nearly ₹1,400 Cr in revenue in calendar year 2025. Yet, Bluetile’s EBITDA remained flat in the quarter despite a 54% revenue jump as the company faced climbing user acquisition costs. Besides all this, the company also faced de-subsidiarisation of its gaming and esports media arm NODWIN Gaming this year. Nazara opted not to participate in a $100 Mn external funding round raised by NODWIN, resulting in its shareholding slipping below 51%. NODWIN is also seeking to list independently on the bourses in the near future. On the financial front, Nazara reported a net loss of ₹82.5 Cr on operating revenue of ₹428.8 Cr in Q1 FY27. The gaming major’s operating revenue also declined 14% YoY to ₹428.8 Cr. title: Whizzo To Raise $26 Mn From Aavishkaar Capital, Bertelsmann
content: Bengaluru-based Whizzo is in talks to raise around $26 Mn in its Series B funding round which could be co-led by Aavishkaar Capital and Bertelsmann Investments (BI), Inc42 learnt. As per sources, existing backers Fundamentum, Lightspeed Ventures, among others, are also likely to participate in the round. Questions sent to Whizzo didn’t elicit any response at the time of publication of the story. The article will be updated based on their responses. The fresh round of funding comes almost six months after the startup raised around $15 Mn in its Series A funding round led by Fundamentum, with participation from Korean investor LB Investment Fund, and Lightspeed. Back then, the startup said it would utilise the funds for strengthening research and development of in-house IP for materials science innovation. Prior to this, Lightspeed Ventures led Whizzo’s seed round in 2025. The Bengaluru-based startup raised its maiden institutional funding round in January 2025 to develop its advanced R&D capabilities, creation of a design lab for fashion-engineered textiles and the expansion of its supply chain. Founded in 2024 by Shrestha Kukreja, Whizzo is a CDMO (contract development and manufacturing organisation) that offers textile design services and textile research & development services to clients across India, Vietnam, China and Bangladesh. The startup integrates R&D, formulation, prototyping, process engineering, and commercial-scale manufacturing under one roof. Whizzo works with B2B manufacturers and produces a wide range of materials for applications across geotextiles, agriculture textiles, protective and flame-retardant materials, specialty yarns, engineered apparel textiles, and industrial composites. It claims to combine sustainability with advanced materials science, offering proprietary textile blends. The potential fundraise comes amid continued investor interest in tech-led textile manufacturing and fabric innovation, as startups look to improve product development and manufacturing processes through proprietary materials and R&D capabilities.
