title: PharmEasy Parent API Holdings’ FY26 Loss Declines 67% YoY To ₹520 Cr
content: PharmEasy parent API Holdings narrowed its consolidated net loss by 67% to ₹520 Cr in the fiscal year ended March 2026 (FY26) from ₹1,572 Cr in the previous fiscal, with its operating revenue growing 12.7% YoY to ₹6,618.5 Cr. The company attributed the improvement to its focus on customer experience, higher-value profitable segments, capacity utilisation, increasing wallet share and leveraging digital capabilities. In its FY26 annual report, API Holdings said it improved margins by focusing on higher-margin products, particularly its private label brands, and optimising discounts in its B2R business. Including other income of ₹70.8 Cr, the company’s total revenue stood at ₹6,689.2 Cr for FY26. However, it continued to report a loss before tax of ₹456.1 Cr. In the first quarter of FY27, API Holdings reported a 10% YoY increase in revenue to ₹1,754 Cr while EBITDA rose to ₹39.3 Cr. Gross margin improved to 21.4% from 19.9% in FY26, and EBITDA margin reached 2.2%. Its B2B business grew 8.2% YoY to ₹1,006 Cr revenue and turned EBITDA-positive at ₹70 lakh. The company said that PharmEasy’s B2C business posted ₹348 Cr revenue, with EBITDA losses narrowing to ₹17 Cr. Thyrocare reported 24% YoY revenue growth to ₹240 Cr, processed 5.4 Mn patients and conducted 55.2 Mn tests. Where Did API Holdings Spend In FY26? API Holdings’ consolidated expenses declined marginally by 0.9% to ₹7,146.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹7,208.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Purchases of stock-in-trade remained its largest expense, while lower employee benefit costs contributed to the overall reduction. Purchases Of Stock-In-Trade: The expense rose 10.9% to ₹5,244.8 Cr from ₹4,729.6 Cr, accounting for about 73% of total expenses. The increase came as the company’s operating revenue expanded during the year. Employee Benefit Expense: Employee costs fell 47.5% to ₹476.9 Cr from ₹908.4 Cr in FY25. A substantial part of the decline came from lower employee share-based payment expenses, which dropped to ₹62 Cr from ₹482.2 Cr in FY25. Other Expenses: This category increased 7.5% YoY to ₹656.7 Cr from ₹610.7 Cr. Major components included ₹111.8 Cr of contractual payments to delivery associates, ₹73.4 Cr of sales promotion and marketing, ₹72.6 Cr of manpower charges, and ₹63.4 Cr of legal and professional fees. API Holdings also reported a tax expense of ₹64.2 Cr, comprising ₹68 Cr in current tax, offset by a deferred tax credit of ₹4.2 Cr, and a prior-period charge of ₹0.4 Cr. Products Account For 86% Of Revenue API Holdings generates revenue from the sale of products and services. Product sales contributed ₹5,670 Cr, or 85.7% of revenue, in FY26. These include pharmaceutical, over-the-counter (OTC), surgical, consumable and private label products. The company sources products from manufacturers and wholesalers and supplies them to local chemists, large pharmacies, doctors, clinics, online retailers on the PharmEasy platform and hospitals. A significant part of this business flows through its chemist-focused distribution operations, while Aknamed supplies hospitals. The group also generates product revenue through collection kits sold by Thyrocare. Services contributed ₹941.3 Cr, or 14.2% of revenue, in FY26. This includes diagnostics, teleconsulting, licensing and technology services. Thyrocare’s diagnostic operations account for a substantial part of this stream, serving franchise partners, consumers, hospitals, diagnostic companies and independent phlebotomists. API Holdings also earns service revenue from diagnostic tests sold through the PharmEasy marketplace, fulfilment services and technology platforms, including Retailio, which connects pharmaceutical wholesalers and pharmacies. How API Holdings’ Subsidiaries Contribute Although API Holdings has six direct subsidiaries and 18 step-down subsidiaries, four businesses account for much of its activity across B2B distribution, diagnostics and consumer healthcare. B2B: Ascent Wellness And Pharma Solutions, Aknamed Ascent Wellness and Pharma Solutions supplies pharmaceutical products to chemists and institutions, sourcing directly from pharmaceutical companies and enabling retailers to place orders through a platform. Aknamed supplies hospitals with pharmaceutical products, consumables and surgical products sourced from pharmaceutical companies and distributors. Together, the B2B businesses generated ₹4,082.4 Cr in revenue in FY26, with an EBITDA loss of ₹3.6 Cr. In Q1 FY27, they recorded combined revenue of ₹1,005.6 Cr and EBITDA of ₹70 Lakh. Diagnostics: Thyrocare Technologies Thyrocare, API Holdings’ listed diagnostics arm, is a key contributor to the group’s profitability. In FY26, it operated 41 laboratories, offered 1,275 tests, processed about 21 Cr tests and had more than 10,800 franchisees. Its revenue grew 24% YoY to ₹240 Cr in Q1 FY27. B2C: PharmEasy PharmEasy operates the group’s consumer-facing healthcare marketplace. In FY26, the segment generated ₹1,334.5 Cr in revenue and reported an EBITDA loss of ₹44.1 Cr. title: Brands Have A New Mission: How To Get AI To Say Your Name
content: “Have you ever clicked your mouse HERE? You will.” That was the text accompanying the first banner ad on the internet, launched by telecommunications company AT&T on HotWired.com in 1994. The ad reportedly clocked a 44% click-through rate in its first four months, a figure that would be extraordinary by the standards of almost any digital marketing channel today. Over three decades, online advertising has evolved from banner ads to search, social media, programmatic buying, influencer marketing and performance marketing. Then, with the emergence of search engine optimisation (SEO) practices, brands started optimising websites, building backlinks, targeting keywords and creating content to improve their visibility. Over time, SEO grew into a $90 Bn industry. But the search box is now changing again. Today, a growing number of consumers are turning to AI assistants instead of typing keywords into Google and opening a dozen links. Whether they are looking for accounting software, a nearby restaurant or the best smartphone under ₹50,000, they can simply ask an AI assistant for recommendations. Their interaction with AI is no longer limited to a query or a list of results. Users/consumers ask follow-up questions, compare options, refine their requirements, and direct AI to recommend what they should buy. This is where answer engine optimisation (AEO) and generative engine optimisation (GEO) have emerged as a new trend. But there is no single platform to optimise for, no standard ranking system and no clear way to measure success. Much like what the SEO function was in its early days, marketers are still figuring out what works. Agencies are experimenting with how brands appear in answers generated by ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google’s AI-powered search products. They are tracking brand mentions, citations and recommendations, while trying to understand why one company gets surfaced over another. But as brands scramble to show up in AI-generated answers, a bigger question is emerging: How can they ensure they are not just recommended by AI, but show up at the right moment? The Missing Link In AI Marketing Currently, for brands, the challenge is not how to appear in AI answers but figure out whether that visibility brings more visitors, customers or sales. Google historically gave marketers detailed visibility through tools such as Search Console and keyword-level paid search data. This model is considerably harder to replicate when consumers interact with AI through multi-step conversations. AI platforms currently offer limited visibility into the prompts driving discovery. A user may start with a broad question, ask several follow-ups, compare products, and only then arrive at a purchase decision. For marketers, identifying which interaction influenced that journey is harder than attributing a click to a specific search query. Organic visibility is also inconsistent across platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity. For queries around the “best” or “top” products and services, AI models may rely heavily on third-party publishers, reviews and user-generated content rather than brand websites. As a result, brands need to build a consistent information ecosystem across websites, ads, influencers and third-party platforms. “So, eventually, for optimising, it becomes a lot more important to produce content in the broader ecosystem. We often ask brands to be consistent with their communication,” said Rishabh Mahendru, senior vice president of client success and growth at AdLift. Marketers are also grappling with how much control they have over their brands’ visibility in AI-driven discovery. AI platforms can answer users’ questions without sending them to an external website. These zero-click answers may be convenient for consumers, but they can reduce traffic to publisher and brand websites. Even when AI search leads to a sale, tracing that purchase back to a specific interaction can be difficult. A consumer may discover a brand through an AI assistant, research it elsewhere and make a purchase days later. Traditional last-click attribution models may fail to capture the role AI played in that journey. There is also less certainty around where and how brands appear. AI platforms determine which ads match a user’s intent, while changes in how models cite sources can make organic visibility unpredictable. Brands also risk appearing alongside misinformation, hate speech or polarising content in AI-generated responses. To address these, OpenAI is exploring geo-based ad experiments and brand-suitability pilots to give advertisers more insight into where their ads appear and how they perform. Overall, with its ChatGPT Ads in India , OpenAI is bringing sponsored messages into conversations on the AI chatbot in one of its largest markets. Ads have been rolled out to users on Free and Go tiers, while Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Education users get an ad-free experience. More than 50 brands were planned to go live during the initial rollout, with WPP and Omnicom as OpenAI’s first agency partners in India. Businesses can access ChatGPT’s self-serve Ads Manager , with daily budgets starting at ₹725. The Next Frontier Of Brand Visibility With no standard way to measure AI search visibility or predict which brands will surface in AI-generated answers, startups are building tools to help businesses navigate the new landscape. Antler-incubated RankinLLM, for instance, is building a GEO and AI search visibility platform. “We operate across three layers: an observability layer to track LLM activity, an intelligence layer to extract meaningful signals from noisy data, and an optimisation layer to fix identified gaps. Optimiser agents create a closed loop, while KPIs such as brand mentions, share of voice, citations and sentiment measure the impact,” said cofounder and CEO Kartik Sharma. Bengaluru-based TruCommerce has taken a different approach. It initially built a tool to track how often brands appeared in AI-generated answers. But it found that much of the traffic coming from AI platforms was being wrongly counted as direct website visits. This led the startup to shift its focus to helping brands sell directly through AI platforms. TruCommerce now connects brands’ product catalogues and inventory with AI assistants. This helps businesses track visitors coming from AI, make product information easier for AI tools to understand, and enable customers to buy products without leaving the conversation. Meanwhile, Lightspeed-backed Gushwork helps small and medium-sized businesses attract potential customers through traditional search engines and AI tools. Its AI agents create content designed to appear in search results, while its platform tracks the enquiries this content generates. Other startups, including Nexad, Parsnip and AdCreative AI, are also building tools to help brands advertise and improve their visibility across AI platforms. For marketers, however, this shift is still in its early stages. Traditional SEO took decades to develop its tools, metrics and best practices. AI is at the same crossroads. title: Deeptech Funding Zooms 2.8X YoY In Q3 Despite Tighter Deal Flow
content: India’s deeptech startups raised substantially more capital in Q3 2026, even as the number of deals edged lower. As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. The 176% YoY increase outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn. For context, deeptech startups are the ones that develop advanced technologies and hardware and include innovations across sub-segments like spacetech, robotics, defence technology and semiconductors. Large Spacetech Rounds Drive Deeptech Funding Surge The sharp rise in funding, despite a marginal decline in deal count, points to a concentration of capital in a smaller pool of startups. In this, large spacetech rounds accounted for a significant share of the funding deployed during the quarter, with the startups in the sector netting $130 Mn, accounting for about 45% of deeptech funding in Q3. Six-year-old spacetech startup Pixxel’s $100 Mn round was one of four mega funding rounds recorded during the quarter. The round accounted for over three-fourths of the segment’s total. Sustaining this momentum will require capital to reach beyond a select group of companies. As per a recent report by the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association (IVCA), deeptech startups continue to face a funding gap at the Series B and C stages, with few funds equipped to write the larger cheques needed to take technologies from development to commercial scale. IVCA President Rajat Tandon said bridging this gap, deepening domestic limited partner participation, and improving exit pathways will be critical to building globally competitive deeptech companies. “India’s deeptech opportunity is moving from promise to more investible commitments, with an increasingly institutionalised ecosystem play. The growth in capital flowing into deeptech over the past decade reflects the confidence investors have in India’s scientific and technological capabilities. However, taking deeptech startups and entrepreneurs from the laboratory to global scale will require capital that is patient, appropriately structured, and available across the entire growth journey,” he said. Government Push Adds To Deeptech Funding Momentum Bharat Innovation Fund cofounder and partner Ashwin Raguraman attributed some of the recent momentum to the government’s ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund and its wider push to support technology-led businesses. “I attribute (growth in deeptech funding) this quarter and maybe even last quarter predominantly due to the announcement on the government’s deeptech-focused ₹1 Lakh Cr RDI Fund and a fairly solid government push, which is making capital available to VC funds,” Raguraman told Inc42. The RDI Fund aims to catalyse private investment in research-intensive businesses. Its framework includes eligibility requirements for R&D-intensive technologies at technology readiness level (TRL) 4 or above, indicating that they have progressed beyond basic laboratory validation. New investment vehicles also emerged during the quarter. Asiana Fund and JC Capital jointly launched a ₹1,000 Cr deeptech fund, while Transition VC and Accel launched funds to back technology-led businesses. Access Free Report RDI Fund Faces Questions Over Governance However, the extent to which the RDI Fund has influenced investor sentiment remains uncertain. In August, The Indian Express reported that nearly two-thirds of the more than ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies under the scheme had gone to firms with links to members of the panel involved in selecting beneficiaries, raising concerns over potential conflicts of interest. Inc42’s Q3 2026 Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, which covered 85 institutional investors, found that 52% considered disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate but said visibility remained limited. Another 25% viewed the issue as a governance failure requiring independent oversight, while 14% said such investment ties could be managed through disclosure and recusal. The remaining 9% said it was not a concern, arguing that the focus should remain on company selection. The findings suggest that the availability of government-backed capital is only part of the equation. Transparency in its allocation and the availability of patient capital across funding stages will also shape the sector’s ability to turn promising technologies into globally competitive businesses. title: D2C Brand Boldfit Raises ₹400 Cr From Bharat Value Fund For Retail Expansion
content: D2C fitness and sportswear brand Boldfit has raised around ₹400 Cr (about $41.8 Mn) from Bharat Value Fund as part of its Series B funding round. The fund is a Category II AIF managed by The Wealth Company Alternates, part of Pantomath Group. Boldfit said the investment would support nationwide retail expansion, product innovation, and manufacturing. It also plans to pursue selective acquisitions to strengthen its presence and capabilities across categories. Founded in 2018 by Pallav Bihani, Bengaluru-based Boldfit sells performance sportswear, athletic footwear, sports equipment, and fitness essentials. The startup claims to serve more than 2 Cr customers annually across India. “We’re building a deeply integrated sports business, investing in product innovation, manufacturing excellence and nationwide retail to create the scale and capabilities required to serve India’s sporting ambitions,” Bihani said. The retail push builds on plans outlined during its ₹110 Cr funding round from Bessemer Venture Partners in November 2024, when Boldfit said it intended to open offline stores over the following 12-18 months. Following the latest round, Boldfit’s total funding to date has risen to over ₹510 Cr. The startup also counts cricketer KL Rahul and former tennis player Sania Mirza among its investors. India’s fitness and sports goods market is estimated to be worth $16 Bn and is projected to reach $35 Bn by FY31, driven by rising disposable incomes, growing health awareness, and wider access through ecommerce, organised retail, and quick commerce channels. As a result, Indian sportswear and athleisure startups are seeing a lot of investor interest. In June, sportswear startup Agilitas raised ₹225 Cr funding round from Nexus Venture Partners and Rainmatter, with Nexus investing ₹200 Cr and Rainmatter contributing ₹25 Cr. In January, D2C athleisure brand CAVA announced a ₹40 Cr Series A round led by Sharrp Ventures, with participation from V3 Ventures and existing investor Spring Marketing Capital. title: How XSCACE Is Taking On Bose And B&O With 12mm-Thin Speakers
content: For decades, names like Bose, Marshall, Bang & Olufsen and KEF have shaped how the world listens to music. Their dominance was built on one simple premise: better sound came from bigger hardware, larger cabinets, larger drivers and speakers designed to be seen and admired. But that premise is increasingly getting at odds with how modern spaces are being designed today. Architects and homeowners are favouring clean walls, minimal interiors and technology that fits seamlessly into the room instead of dominating it. The shift has put one of consumer electronics’ oldest categories in a difficult spot: speakers. Good quality speakers need physical space to deliver the depth, power and clarity that listeners expect. Manufacturers have tried to shrink the hardware, but making it smaller meant compromising on sound quality that made the product desirable in the first place — a trade-off the industry has largely lived with rather than solved. For Utkarsh Hora, the cofounder of Canadian architectural audio startup XSCACE , audio was part of his family history. His grandfather, Bansi Lal Hora, had worked with Philips in Thailand before returning to India, where he began repairing high-end audio equipment. His father, Manoj Hora, carried that experience forward, building a business around premium audio installations. For Utkarsh, speakers and audio systems were therefore less a hobby than a part of everyday life. During his time at the University of Toronto, he began wondering whether high-performance audio really needed to take up so much space. The question eventually became the starting point for XSCACE, which Utkarsh founded in 2022. He set out to build speakers that could deliver high-quality sound without taking over a room or compromising its design. The challenge, however, was rooted in a fundamental constraint of speaker design known as Hoffman’s Iron Law. According to the law, a designer can optimise for only two of three things at once: deep bass, a small enclosure and high efficiency. XSCACE’s challenge was to push the boundaries of that trade-off without compromising the quality of sound. After two years of development and testing, XSCACE made its first commercial sale in January 2024. Today, the brand has a range of ultra-compact speakers built around six proprietary technologies. It is expanding its distribution across international markets. How XSCACE Is Reinventing The Wheel When Utkarsh started his entrepreneurial journey, he observed that modern luxury spaces were becoming increasingly minimal. Architects and interior designers wanted clean walls, hidden wiring and fewer visible fixtures. Speakers, however, remained stubbornly hard to hide. In-wall and in-ceiling speakers existed, but they often came with a compromise. Products that blended into the architecture could fall short on sound, while speakers built for stronger performance typically needed more space. The fundamental challenge stemmed from a long-standing principle of speaker design known as Hoffman’s Iron Law. It describes the trade-off between a speaker’s size, bass response and efficiency. Improving one typically means giving up something elsewhere. Rather than accept the rules as they were, the founder began by rethinking what sat at the speaker’s centre: the driver. In a sense, Utkarsh was trying to reinvent the wheel. Instead of optimising individual components in isolation, XSCACE approached the speaker as one interconnected system. Driver geometry, motor design, cone materials, crossover architecture, cabinet construction and thermal management were developed together, with each element designed to work within the constraints of the others. “We didn’t eliminate the trade-off altogether but became far more intentional about where it exists,” the founder said. This paved the way for the foundation of six proprietary technologies, each tackling a different part of the performance equation. These are as follows: Nano Resonance: To focus on ultra-compact driver performance PowerDense Dynamics: Extracts higher output from miniature motors AeroFrame Chassis: Reduces resonance PrecisionXover Array: Solves for seamless driver integration XS-Flow: For Airflow and bass response PsySculpt: Creates a more convincing spatial experience through psychoacoustic tuning “ Among these, Nano Resonance was one of the hardest pieces to develop,” the founder said, adding that the challenge was to get deep bass, high output and low distortion from a miniature driver while maintaining long-term reliability. From Prototype To Production A prototype that performs exceptionally in controlled conditions does not automatically translate into a product that can be manufactured consistently. So the next big task was to turn that engineering into a product that could be manufactured consistently without losing performance. The founder had to revisit parts of the product with manufacturability and repeatability in mind. “It’s one thing to build a prototype and altogether a different ball game to build the exact same product at scale,” he said. While spending on simulation, prototyping, testing and refinement across acoustics, mechanical design, materials and manufacturing, the founder had to build a multidisciplinary team and invest in engineering capabilities. After rigorous experimentation, testing and improving the designs, the founder was finally able to turn its two products, Bonsai and Cane, from early experimental concepts into actual products that were ready to be manufactured and sold. Bonsai: An ultra-slim, compact speaker that is just 12 mm deep and delivers 40W. It is designed to be mounted discreetly on walls or installed in walls or ceilings. Cane: A slightly larger 23 mm-thin slim-array speaker with 50W output, designed for spaces where you want more output while keeping the speaker visually unobtrusive. Building More Than Speakers Utkarsh’s quest didn’t end with making speakers compact and minimal. From the outset, he saw software as an extension of his product lineup. “I did not want our products to depend entirely on third-party software,” he said. Therefore, he started developing an in-house software ecosystem. Today, the brand offers an AI Configurator to help architects, designers and integrators plan and configure audio systems, alongside a companion app for users and the Xylem DSP Controller, which lets installers fine-tune sound based on a room’s acoustics. Over time, the AI Configurator is expected to become more than a planning tool. Utkarsh sees it evolving into a broader platform that can support installation, calibration, optimisation and ongoing system management. The software strategy also reflects where he wants to take XSCACE as a business. “Our five-year vision is to establish XSCACE as a global reference in premium architectural audio,” he said, adding that broader plans include expanding beyond loudspeakers into software, DSP, amplification and complementary products, while strengthening its presence in India and expanding across the US, Europe and the Middle East. For him, growth is not just about revenue or entering more markets. He measures the brand’s progress through its engineering, intellectual property, product consistency and the trust it builds with architects, integrators and customers. In many ways, that brings XSCACE back to the problem that started it. The brand did not set out simply to build smaller speakers. It wanted to challenge the assumption that high-performance audio had to remain visible. Now, as XSCACE moves from compact architectural speakers towards a broader audio ecosystem, the original idea remains at the centre of the brand: build small, think big and make every inch punch above its weight. title: Indian Startup IPO Tracker 2026
content: Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets . The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “⁠Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, fifteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty six startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub. With much on the anvil, we have compiled a list of Indian new-age tech companies eyeing a Dalal Street debut later this year. Capital, SBI Capital Markets, DAM Capital Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026 AceVector Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector traces its roots to 2010, when the duo founded ecommerce platform Snapdeal. Over the years, this umbrella company expanded to include listed ecommerce enablement startup Unicommerce and house of brands Stellaro Brands. The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, AceVector filed its confidential DRHP with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in July 2025. The regulator greenlit the offering in November 2025. Almost a year later in September 2026, AceVector filed its red herring prospectus with the SEBI , which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS component of up to 4.16 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share , valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. Subsequently, AceVector’s public issue was oversubscribed 4.93X, receiving bids for 36.61 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer. The company eventually made a weak debut on the exchanges on October 5. Shares of AceVector listed at ₹28.30 on the BSE, a discount of 11.6% to its issue price of ₹32 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹28.32, an 11.5% discount to the IPO price. On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹395 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, losses also shrank nearly 64% to ₹ 45.5 Cr versus ₹126.3 Cr in FY25. Amagi Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services. The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹ 816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X . The company had set a price band of ₹ 343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹ 7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges . The stock listed at ₹ 317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹ 361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹ 318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price. Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹ 6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹ 66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹ 704.8 Cr. Aye Finance Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO. In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO , which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97% , with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses , listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26 , while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. ESDS Software Solution Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida. The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh. Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025. As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consisted solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr . Its public issue, which stretched between August 28 and September 1, closed with an oversubscription of 135.88X . Subsequently, shares of the company made a stellar debut on the bourses , listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over the issue price of ₹429. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹746.30, marking a gain of nearly 74% over the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25. Fractal Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn. In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI , and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X , with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900. On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26 , while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. Kissht Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property. The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast. The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X. Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. Klassroom Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country. The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO , which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr . Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X. Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170 , a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25. LEAP India A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON. LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures. The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility. Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025 . In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO , which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer. Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE. Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25. Moneyview Founded in 2016 by Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, Moneyview started off as a personal finance platform before pivoting to digital lending. Today, it offers services such as UPI payments, gold SIPs, fixed deposits, digital gold, home loans, BNPL and insurance. The company claims to manage over ₹19,800 Cr in AUM and has raised more than $250 Mn in funding. It competes with players like listed fintech MobiKwik, IPO-aspirant Navi, and MoneyTap. It entered the unicorn club in 2024. In March 2026, the fintech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO. It then received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in late-June 2026. In September 2026, the fintech unicorn filed its RHP. outlining an IPO with a fresh issue of shares worth ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of up to 10.04 Cr equity shares. The startup’s public issue then closed with an oversubscription of 98.46X , led by QIBs and NIIs. The digital lender made a bumper debut on the exchanges on October 1, with its shares listing at ₹55.6 on the BSE, a premium of 64% over the issue price of ₹34. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹55, marking a premium of nearly 62% over the issue price. Moneyview’s operating revenue grew 43.3% to ₹3,351.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,339.1 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, net profit rose a marginal 1% to ₹242.7 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹240.3 Cr in FY25. Purple Style Labs Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury house of brands featuring fashion labels like Pernia’s Pop Up Studio & Shop, Wendell Rodricks, and Hemant Trevedi. It operates over 12 Pernia’s Pop-Up Studio experience centres across India. Backed by Alchemy Capital Management, Bajaj Holdings and Investment, and Minerva Ventures, the startup has raised more than $78 Mn to date. In September 2025, the D2C brand filed its DRHP with SEBI for its public issue and received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. It then filed its RHP with SEBI in August 2026 for a public issue, which consisted entirely of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component. Subsequently, Purple Style Labs’ public issue opened for subscription in late August 2026 and closed with an oversubscription of 1.29X, receiving bids for 88.54 Lakh shares against 68.49 Lakh shares on offer. Shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on September 7. The stock listed at ₹535 on the NSE, 6.96% lower than the issue price of ₹575. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹539, representing a discount of 6.26%. On the financial front, the startup’s consolidated net loss widened 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 as against ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue for the fiscal rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25. RentoMojo Founded in 2014 by Geetansh Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo is an omnichannel rental platform to lease appliances, furniture, and furnishings. The startup operates an app, website and physical stores. It operates 20 warehouses and 82 offline stores across 29 cities. Backed by Accel, Chiratae Ventures and Bain Capital, the startup has raised over $45 Mn in funding to date. Hopping on the IPO bandwagon in March 2026, the rental platform filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO and received SEBI’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026. In September 2026, the startup finally filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.7 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹384-₹404 per share for its IPO. The public issue opened for bidding on September 9 and closed on September 11. The IPO was oversubscribed 72.88X , receiving bids for 158.68 Cr shares against the 2.18 Cr shares on offer. Shares of RentoMojo made a strong stock market debut on September 17. The stock listed at ₹482.45 on the NSE, a premium of 19.42% over its issue price of ₹404. On the BSE, RentoMojo opened at ₹480, up 18.81% from the issue price. The IPO opened despite RentoMojo cofounder and former COO Nain earlier filing a petition before the NCLT’s Bengaluru bench to stall the IPO proceedings. Alleging oppression and mismanagement, the plea claimed that incomplete or inaccurate information was shared with him and sought to declare his 2023 sale of 2,223 shares void ab initio. On the financial front, RentoMojo reported a profit after tax of ₹104.3 Cr in FY26, up 142% from ₹43.1 Cr in the previous fiscal, aided by a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr during the year under review from ₹266 Cr in FY25. SEDEMAC Founded in 2007 by IIT-Bombay professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Amit Dixit, and Manish Sharma, SEDMAC designs electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications. The deeptech company produces motor control units, integrated starter generators, fuel injection systems, genset controllers, and small industrial powertrains. Backed by Xponentia Capital Partners, A91 Partners, and 360 ONE Asset, SEDMAC has raised over $107 Mn to date. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the deeptech company filed its DRHP with SEBI in November 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in February 2026. Its public issue comprised solely an OFS component of up to 80.43 Lakh shares. The IPO was oversubscribed 2.68X , with investors cumulatively bidding for 1.51 Cr shares against 56.32 Lakh shares on offer. Shares of the company made a stellar debut on the exchanges on March 11, listing at a premium of 13.5% on the NSE. The stock opened at ₹1,535 as against the issue price of ₹1,352 per share. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹1,510, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price. SEDEMAC reported a net profit of ₹71.4 Cr in the first nine months of FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹770.66 Cr during the period under review. Shadowfax Founded in 2015 by Vaibhav Khandelwal and Abhishek Bansal, Shadowfax is a logistics company that offers hyperlocal and on-demand delivery solutions for businesses. Competing with the likes of Delhivery, LoadShare and Pickrr, the logistics major is backed by names such as Flipkart, Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India), IFC, Nokia Growth Partners, Qualcomm and Trifecta Capital. Shadowfax pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 for an IPO, and received markets regulator’s nod in October 2025. It filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in November 2025. The company’s IPO comprised a fresh issue worth ₹ 1,000 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹ 907 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.72X , receiving total bids for 24.23 Cr shares against 8.9 Cr on offer. Subsequently, shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on January 28. The stock listed at ₹ 112.60 apiece on the NSE, a discount of 9.19% to the issue price of ₹ 124. On the BSE, shares of the logistics unicorn debuted at ₹ 113, down 8.87% below the issue price. In H1 FY26, the logistics unicorn’s net profit more than doubled to ₹ 21 Cr from ₹ 9.8 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue surged 68.4% YoY to ₹ 1,805.6 Cr during the period. Shiprocket Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Vishesh Khurana, Akshay Gulati, and Gautam Kapoor, Shiprocket aggregates third-party logistics providers. It claims to partner 17 courier firms like Delhivery, FedEx, Aramex, Xpressbees, DTDC, and Shadowfax and serves over 24,000 pin codes across India. The logistics unicorn has raised over $323 Mn to date from investors like Temasek, Bertelsmann, Tribe Capital, Lightrock, and Zomato. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the Zomato-backed unicorn in May 2025 confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI and received the regulator’s approval in October 2025. Shiprocket then filed its RHP with the markets regulator in August 2026. The logistics major’s ₹1,617 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹885.5 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹732 Cr. Subsequently, in mid-August 2026, Shiprocket’s public issue opened to healthy market response and closed with an oversubscription of 99.38X , receiving bidding for 938.53 Cr shares against 9.44 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a strong debut on the D-Street on August 19. The stock listed at ₹131 on the NSE, marking a premium of 35.05% to the issue price of ₹97. On the BSE, it debuted at ₹129.50, a premium of 33.51%. On the financial front, Shiprocket’s operating revenue rose 24% to ₹2,024 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,632 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, net loss widened over 6% to ₹79.2 Cr during the fiscal from ₹74.5 Cr in FY25. Turtlemint Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurtech platform that enables financial advisors to distribute car, bike, health, and term life insurance to their customer networks. It claims to serve over 3 Lakh advisors nationwide. The startup has raised more than $197 Mn to date from investors such as Amansa Capital, Jungle Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Vitruvian Partners, and Nexus Venture Partners. In September 2025, Turtlemint pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI, and secured market regulator’s approval three months later in December. Subsequently, the insurtech unicorn filed its RHP in June 2026. The IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹660.7 Cr and an OFS of 1.46 Cr shares. Its public issue opened on June 19 and closed on June 23, with an oversubscription of 1.2X . Despite this, the startup made a muted debut on the bourses on June 29. Shares of the insurtech startup listed at ₹134.90 on the NSE, a discount of 11.25% to the issue price of ₹152. On the BSe, the stock listed at ₹136.2 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 10.4% to the issue price. The insurtech company’s net loss rose 19% to ₹184.7 Cr in the first nine months (9M) of FY26 as against a net loss of ₹154.7 Cr in the year-ago period. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 80% to ₹741.1 Cr from ₹411.1 Cr in 9M FY25. Startups That Have Filed DRHP Atomberg Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg began as a B2B supplier of energy-efficient BLDC fans before entering the D2C segment in 2016. It has since expanded to manufacture mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances. The startup designs and manufactures its products in India and sells them via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. Backed by names such as Steadview Capital, Jungle Ventures and A91 Partners, Atomberg has raised over $126 Mn in funding to date. Taking the first step towards its public listing, the D2C appliance brand, in July 2026, converted into a public entity and changed the name of its parent entity from Atomberg Technologies Pvt Ltd to Atomberg Technologies Ltd. In August 2026, the startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO , which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an OFS of up to 7.65 Cr shares. The startup is also considering raising up to ₹90 Cr through a pre-IPO placement. On the financial front, Atomberg’s losses widened 26.5% to ₹149 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹117.8 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 34.8% to ₹1,293.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹959.5 Cr in FY25. AVPL International (AITMC Ventures) Founded in 2016 by Preet Sandhuu and Deep Sisai, AITMC sits at the intersection of agriculture and drones.
